The radio in her earpiece had gone dead a minute ago—first a hiss, then nothing but the soft pressure of plastic against skin. In the stairwell, footsteps multiplied into a steady, practiced drumbeat. Not running. Not panicked. The kind of pace men kept when they knew every exit was already covered.

She stood with her back to the concrete wall, breathing through her nose to keep the sound down, tasting metal and dust. The service door at the bottom of the stairs was chained. The door above was already opening—slow, controlled, as if whoever held the handle wanted her to hear the inevitability of it.

Her fingers found the seam in her collar without looking. The capsule was tucked where a tailor would have hidden a spare button, wrapped in wax and fabric. For a moment it felt absurdly small, like a bead. Like something meant to be swallowed by mistake.

Her thumb pressed it into her palm.

The door above clicked fully shut again. A voice carried down, calm and amused, in a language she’d spent years learning to speak without an accent.

“Don’t make this difficult.”

She didn’t answer. There were a dozen things she could have said—names, bargaining chips, the lie that she’d cooperate. All of them took time. All of them assumed she still had any to spend.

She lifted the capsule to her mouth. The old, drilled protocol rose in her mind with the flat certainty of a checklist: *If captured, you become a weapon in their hands.* Her own body, turned into a lever. Her own voice, pressed into giving them what they wanted.

She bit down.

It didn’t crunch like bone or glass. It gave with a thin, papery resistance, and then the taste hit—sharp and bitter, as if she’d cracked open a battery on her tongue. Her throat tightened instinctively, trying to reject it, and for a half-second panic flared bright and stupid: *Spit it out.* It was pure animal reflex, the part of her that wanted nothing more sophisticated than to keep breathing.

She swallowed anyway.

The bitterness slid down her throat and seemed to coat the inside of her chest. It wasn’t dramatic at first; there was no cinematic thunderclap. There was only an immediate wrongness, as if some essential switch had been turned and her body hadn’t yet been told why.

Her pulse jumped, then stuttered into a frantic, uneven rhythm she could feel in her neck, in her wrists, in the soft tissue behind her eyes. Air went in, but it stopped feeling like it did anything. Each breath became an action without result—lungs obeying orders, blood no longer listening.

The stairwell shifted. The concrete walls, the hazard stripes, the handrail—everything sharpened for a moment, too bright, too detailed, and then the edges began to blur. Heat flushed up her face and then drained away in a cold sweep that left her fingertips numb. Her tongue went thick in her mouth. Saliva gathered and she had to swallow again, harder this time, to keep from coughing.

Above her, boots started down the stairs.

She took one step, then another, as if her legs might remember their job even if the rest of her didn’t. Her knees trembled, not from fear but from a sudden weakness that felt structural, as if someone had unbolted her from the inside.

She pressed her shoulder to the wall to steady herself. The concrete was cold through her shirt, oddly comforting in its solidity. Her hearing narrowed to a tunnel: the boots, her own breathing, the faint thump of her heart trying to keep pace with a body that was slipping away from it.

A thought arrived with a clarity that was almost clinical.

*This is it.*

Not a metaphor. Not a rehearsal. Not something she could negotiate around with discipline and training. The end wasn’t a dramatic curtain; it was a door closing, quietly, on the other side of which there were no more choices.

She tried to take a deeper breath and discovered she couldn’t make it satisfying. It was like drinking water that never reached thirst. A pressure built behind her sternum. Her vision dimmed at the edges, the center remaining bright for a few moments longer, as if the world were insisting on being seen until the last possible second.

The footsteps were closer now. A silhouette appeared at the turn in the stairs—shoulders, weapon, the shine of a flashlight beam searching her face.

“Hands where I can—”

His command trailed off, not because he softened, but because he saw it: the slackening control around her eyes, the way she was bracing herself against the wall like someone pretending to stand. His light caught the sheen of sweat on her upper lip, the slight tremor at the corner of her mouth.

She wanted to speak—to give him something final, something sharp—but her throat wouldn’t coordinate with language anymore. The muscles that formed words were becoming unfamiliar, as if they belonged to someone else.

The cold realization wasn’t fear. Fear had always been loud, full of scenarios and escapes. This was quieter. This was accounting.

Faces flickered through her mind without permission: a handler’s hands sliding a dossier across a table; a friend laughing in a safehouse kitchen; the man she’d used, and the one who’d used her; a city at night seen through rain on a window. Not guilt, not nostalgia—just inventory, as if the mind, understanding it was being evicted, was taking one last walk through the rooms.

The radio in her earpiece had gone dead a minute ago—first a hiss, then nothing but the soft pressure of plastic against skin. In the stairwell, footsteps multiplied into a steady, practiced drumbeat. Not running. Not panicked. The kind of pace men kept when they knew every exit was already covered.

She stood with her back to the concrete wall, breathing through her nose to keep the sound down, tasting metal and dust. The service door at the bottom of the stairs was chained. The door above was already opening—slow, controlled, as if whoever held the handle wanted her to hear the inevitability of it.

Her fingers found the seam in her collar without looking. The capsule was tucked where a tailor would have hidden a spare button, wrapped in wax and fabric. For a moment it felt absurdly small, like a bead. Like something meant to be swallowed by mistake.

Her thumb pressed it into her palm.

The door above clicked fully shut again. A voice carried down, calm and amused, in a language she’d spent years learning to speak without an accent.

“Don’t make this difficult.”

She didn’t answer. There were a dozen things she could have said—names, bargaining chips, the lie that she’d cooperate. All of them took time. All of them assumed she still had any to spend.

She lifted the capsule to her mouth. The old, drilled protocol rose in her mind with the flat certainty of a checklist: If captured, you become a weapon in their hands. Her own body, turned into a lever. Her own voice, pressed into giving them what they wanted.

Her throat tightened instinctively, trying to reject it, and for a half-second panic flared bright and stupid: Spit it out. She swallowed anyway.

The bitterness slid down her throat and seemed to coat the inside of her chest. It wasn’t dramatic at first; there was no cinematic thunderclap. There was only an immediate wrongness, as if some essential switch had been turned and her body hadn’t yet been told why.

Her pulse jumped, then stuttered into a frantic, uneven rhythm she could feel in her neck, in her wrists, in the soft tissue behind her eyes. Air went in, but it stopped feeling like it did anything. Each breath became an action without result—lungs obeying orders, blood no longer listening.

The scene settles into a strange stillness once the motion stops—an absence where the engine’s howl and tire noise should be. What’s left is scattered evidence of speed: a helmet lying at an angle with fresh scrapes ground into the shell, a glove a few yards away, plastic fairing shards and mirror glass glittering across the asphalt like dirty confetti. The motorcycle itself usually ends up farther than you’d expect, on its side, leaking fluids in a widening dark stain while metal ticks as it cools. A thin, chalky trail of abraded rubber and gouged pavement marks the line it took, and you can see where parts hit, skipped, and hit again.

In the quiet, small sounds become prominent—wind moving through roadside grass, distant traffic that hasn’t realized what happened yet, the occasional ping from hot metal. Dust hangs low, and the air can carry a sharp mix of fuel, hot oil, and burnt rubber. Nothing moves for a moment except loose paper or plastic lifting and settling with each gust.

The rider’s body tells the story in blunt, physical terms. “Road rash” at high speed isn’t a simple scrape; it’s a broad, abraded area where layers of skin have been rubbed away by the pavement, often patterned with embedded grit and tiny fragments from the road. The affected areas can look raw and swollen, with torn fabric stuck to them where clothing failed, and the surrounding skin already tightening and reddening as shock and inflammation set in. Even when bleeding isn’t dramatic, the surface damage can be extensive, and the pain tends to be delayed and then overwhelming as nerves catch up.

Broken limbs often present as unnatural angles or positions that don’t match how a joint should rest. An arm may be tucked oddly beneath the torso, or a leg turned outward too far, the limb rigid or slack in a way that suggests the structure underneath isn’t holding. Swelling can start quickly, and the rider may be very still—not necessarily from calm, but from the body’s protective shutdown—breathing shallowly, eyes unfocused, or trying not to move because every shift sends new pain through injured bones and scraped skin.

The overall impression is contrast: the violence of what just happened is gone, replaced by debris, skid marks, and a quiet that makes the rider’s injuries feel even more stark and immediate. If this is for a story, I can tailor the description to a specific setting (highway at night, mountain road, urban intersection) and the rider’s gear (leathers vs. jeans, full-face helmet vs. half).

results.model_response:
The woods had a way of making every sound belong to you.

My breath, for one. Too loud. Too close. I tried to pull it back into my chest like I could hide it there, but it kept spilling out in pale bursts that turned to ghosts and vanished between the trees. Somewhere behind me, something moved with the patience of a hunter that didn’t need to hurry.

A twig snapped.

I stopped so hard my boots skidded on the damp leaves. The night pressed in, heavy with the scent of wet bark and cold soil. The trail I’d been following—if you could call a narrow strip of flattened fern a trail—was gone. Every direction looked the same: black trunks, silvered branches, patches of fog clinging low as wool.

Another snap, closer.

I turned slowly, lifting my flashlight with a hand that had gone numb from gripping it too hard. The beam cut through the mist and found nothing but the thick spine of a spruce.

Then a shape shifted at the edge of the light. Not stepping into it, not yet—just enough movement to tell my eyes they weren’t imagining it. A shoulder? A head? It was hunched low, built like a man trying to crawl on all fours, as if standing up would be too conspicuous.

My mouth dried. “Who’s there?”

No answer. Only the soft, steady sound of something breathing, timed with my own but deeper, slower—as if the forest itself had lungs.

I backed away. The leaves under my heel gave a wet, sucking sound. The shape moved to match me without making a matching sound. It didn’t hurry. It didn’t need to. I could feel it calculating every step I took.

I swung the light wider, forcing it. The beam caught fur—dark and mottled, not quite black, not quite brown. For a heartbeat it was just an animal crouched in the ferns. Then the eyes reflected back, too high, too forward-facing, too knowing.

Human eyes in an animal face.

My stomach turned over.

It shifted again, and I finally saw the outline: long forelimbs bent wrong for a wolf, jointed like arms trying to be legs. A torso too upright. A head too broad in the jaw, the muzzle shortened as if someone had started to carve a wolf out of a man and stopped halfway.

It watched me like it understood language and simply didn’t care to use it.

I stumbled back and hit a tree. Bark bit through my coat. The flashlight beam jerked and skated across trunks. For a second the light pointed down, catching only my own boots and the frantic tremble of my knees.

When I raised it again, the thing was gone from where it had been.

Panic hit like a physical shove. I pushed off the tree and ran.

Branches slapped my face. The forest floor dipped and rose, grabbing at my feet with roots and moss. My lungs burned, the cold sharpening every breath into a knife. Behind me, there was no crashing pursuit, no panting gallop.

Just the certainty of being followed.

I burst into a small clearing without meaning to. A ring of birches stood around it like pale pillars, their bark bright in the flashlight’s spill. The clearing was wrong—too open, too quiet, the kind of space the woods made only when it wanted you visible.

I stopped, trying to listen, trying not to be loud enough to hear myself.

A low sound rolled out of the dark. Not a growl—not yet. More like a throat clearing itself of humanity.

The hair on my arms lifted. I turned in a slow circle, the flashlight beam sweeping, searching.

It stepped into the light on the far side of the clearing.

At first glance it was a man. Tall, hunched, bare-headed, shoulders too wide under a torn coat that hung in strips. Its hands hung at its sides, fingers flexing as if it were angry or cold. It took a step, and I saw the way its boots didn’t fit right, as though the feet inside were already changing shape.

Then the head tipped up and the light caught its face.

The skin was drawn tight over the cheekbones, eyes set too deep. The mouth was closed, but the lips had a strained look, pulled as if something beneath them was pushing forward. The nose flared. It inhaled, and its chest expanded with a shudder that traveled through its whole frame.

It found me by scent, not sight. The eyes met mine anyway, and I knew it could see my fear as clearly as the beam of my flashlight.

I tried to speak—anything, a plea, a threat, a prayer—but my throat refused.

The man-thing took another step, and that was when the first crack sounded.

A sharp, brittle report that didn’t belong to the forest.

It flinched as if struck from within. Its shoulders jerked up. The coat shifted on its back, and I saw the fabric strain, seams pulling apart a fraction.

Another crack. Louder.

It folded forward, one hand bracing on its knee. The other hand curled into a fist so hard the knuckles blanched under the pale skin. Its breathing changed—ragged, forced through clenched teeth.

Then the clenched teeth weren’t teeth anymore.

The mouth opened in a grimace, and I watched the jaw push outward, not smoothly like a mask being pulled on, but in jolts, as if the bones were arguing with the shape they were being made to take. The skin around its cheeks stretched, tightening, shining faintly in my light. Its lips split at the corners, the line of the mouth widening against its will.

A wet, horrible sound came from its throat—half strangled groan, half animal noise—and it snapped its mouth shut as if trying to hold itself together.

It didn’t work.

Its spine bowed, vertebrae shifting under the coat in a visible ripple. The movement was wrong, too segmented, like someone running their hands along a zipper under fabric. The shoulders rose higher, the collarbones pushing up until the coat’s collar dug in and tore. Its neck thickened, cords standing out as if the muscles were swelling in fast motion.

Crack.

The sound came from its arm. I saw the forearm twist, the wrist bending inward. It cried out—no, it tried to, but the sound that came was deeper and rougher, breaking apart as its throat reshaped around it. The fingers splayed, and the bones inside them seemed to lengthen, joint by joint, as if each one had to break and re-set to accommodate the new size. The nails darkened and thickened, curving into points that caught my flashlight and flashed.

I couldn’t look away. My body had decided that if it understood what was happening, it could survive it.

The coat gave up entirely at the back with a tearing sound. Beneath it, the skin shifted as if something were crawling under it, spreading. Hair erupted in patches, first thin, then dense, swallowing the pale flesh in a dark pelt that crawled up the spine and over the shoulders. It wasn’t a gentle growth; it came with the pull of skin stretching to make room, the surface of the body tightening and then loosening like fabric being yanked into a new shape.

Its chest expanded again, wider, deeper. Ribs pressed outward, not in a slow breath but in a forced reshaping. The fabric across its torso ripped in a line, and for a brief, sickening second I saw the way the skin was pulled taut over shifting muscle, the contours changing as if someone were molding it with brute hands.

The head dipped. The skull seemed to swell behind the brow, and the forehead sloped as the face pushed forward. The nose flattened, then extended, cartilage and bone rearranging in tiny, snapping increments. The ears—human, close to the head—climbed upward, lengthening, sharpening into points through a series of small cracks I could hear even from across the clearing.

Its eyes stayed fixed on me the whole time, and that was the worst of it. They didn’t glaze over. They didn’t turn mindless. They watched, enduring the transformation like a man enduring a fire, and there was something in that gaze that said it was choosing this.

It dropped to one knee, hands digging into the dirt. The fingers sank in like hooks. Its shoulders rolled, arms thickening, the elbows shifting backward as the joints realigned. The sound of it—bone complaining, tendons tightening, breath turning into a rumble—filled the clearing until the forest felt small and trapped around us.

Then it lurched up on all fours.

The movement looked almost like relief, like the new shape fit better. The spine settled into a long, powerful curve. The legs kicked out behind it, and I heard the boots tear as the feet inside them lengthened, toes splitting into a new arrangement, the heel lifting until the ankle became something else entirely. It shook once, as if trying to throw off the last scraps of human balance.

When it raised its head again, the flashlight beam caught a muzzle slick with saliva, lips pulled back from teeth that had become too many and too sharp. The tongue tasted the air. The breath came out in a steaming gust that carried the smell of wet fur and iron.

It stood.

Not fully upright like a man—too tall for that now—but it rose high enough that its head was level with my own, even across the distance. Its forelimbs hung with the wrong kind of intelligence, paws that were still hands if you looked too closely. The chest was massive, fur bristling. The neck was thick with muscle. The eyes, still those same eyes, narrowed.

The werewolf took one slow step forward. Claws clicked softly on a stone at the edge of the clearing, a sound delicate enough to be polite.

I realized I’d been holding my breath. I let it out, and it seemed to hear that too. Its nostrils flared. Its head tilted, as if listening to my heart through my ribs.

My legs finally remembered their job. I backed away, flashlight shaking so badly the beam jittered across its body. The werewolf didn’t rush. It only watched me retreat, head tracking, as calm as a shadow.

I turned to run again, and the last thing I heard before the darkness swallowed the clearing was the soft, deliberate crunch of leaves behind me—one step, unhurried.

It was coming.

And it was enjoying the time it took.

results.model_response:
The fever had started an hour ago.

It always started like that, Mara had told them—like the body knew before the mind admitted it. A heat under the skin, a shiver that didn’t match the temperature. Then the tremor in the hands. Then the eyes, going glassy as if someone had poured a thin film over the world.

Jonah sat with his back against the overturned desk, legs stretched out, boot soles dusty and still. The bite was on his forearm, wrapped in cloth so tight it looked like it hurt more than the teeth had. Dark seepage had already freckled the bandage. His jaw worked as if he were chewing something bitter. His breath came short, but measured, as though he could bargain with his lungs.

Outside the boarded windows, something dragged itself along the brick. A soft, persistent scrape. The building answered with a slow creak, settling into itself like an old animal.

Mara knelt in front of him with her hands on her thighs. She’d been the one to check the wound—fast, competent, mercilessly honest. She’d been the one to say, “It’s deep,” and then to go quiet, because there was nothing else to say that wouldn’t be pretending.

Silas stood a few steps back, near the door, a rifle held but not raised. His fingers kept adjusting on the stock like he couldn’t find a grip that didn’t make him feel guilty. He stared at the floorboards, at a knot in the wood, at anything that wasn’t Jonah’s face.

Leena hovered by the shelves, still clutching the scavenged medical bag as if it could become a miracle if she squeezed hard enough. Her eyes were red, though she was making a fierce, rigid effort not to let it spill over into tears. Tears took water. Tears took time. Tears did nothing.

Jonah’s voice came out rough. “So.” He looked at each of them in turn, and it was the looking that hurt the most—how present he still was. How much him there was left. “We doing this or what?”

Mara’s throat moved. “We need to talk.”

Jonah’s laugh was a single breath. “No. You need to talk.”

Leena took a step forward, the medical bag dangling from her fingers. “Maybe—maybe it’s not—”

Mara’s head turned sharply. Not angry. Worse. Tired. “Leena.”

Leena’s mouth opened, closed. Her gaze flicked to Jonah’s bandaged arm, then away. “We’ve never… we’ve never waited it out with someone who—who had a chance to—” She swallowed. “To say anything.”

“Chances,” Jonah echoed. His eyelids fluttered, and he steadied himself with the heel of his hand pressed to his forehead. “That’s funny.”

Silas finally lifted his eyes. “Jonah…”

Jonah angled his head, as if listening. The scrape outside came again, accompanied by a distant, wet sigh. Jonah’s expression tightened.

“It’s already pulling on me,” he said quietly. “You hear that? That part of my brain that used to just be me is… turning into a room with a door that won’t close.”

Leena’s voice broke. “Stop.”

“I’m not trying to scare you,” Jonah said, immediately softer, like he was smoothing a sheet over a child. “I’m trying to save you the part where you pretend you don’t know what happens next.”

Mara’s hands had curled into fists. When she spoke, her voice was flat from effort. “We have protocols.”

“Protocols.” Jonah nodded. “Right.”

Silas shifted his weight. The rifle strap creaked, loud in the silence. “We can restrain you. If you want time. If you want—” He swallowed, and the word wouldn’t come. If you want to say goodbye. As if there was a clean way to do that.

Jonah looked at him. His eyes were still his: a green that had always seemed too gentle for the things they’d had to do. “You really want to be the guy who ties me up and listens to me choke on my own name until it’s gone?”

Silas flinched as though struck.

Mara’s gaze dropped to Jonah’s arm. “How long since the bite?”

“Two hours,” Jonah said. “Give or take. Does it matter?”

“It matters,” Mara murmured, and then she faltered, because it didn’t. The question was a habit, a way to put numbers around something that refused to become manageable.

Leena sank down on a crate, the medical bag thumping against the floor. She pressed her palms to her eyes hard enough to blanch the skin. When she spoke, her words were muffled. “I can’t.”

Jonah reached out with his unbitten hand, slow, deliberate. His fingers touched her knee lightly, a weight that asked permission.

Leena uncovered her face and looked at him. The rawness in her expression made her seem younger than she was. “I’m sorry,” she whispered, as if she were the one dying. As if apology could be a rope thrown across a canyon.

“I know,” Jonah said. “I know you are.”

Mara inhaled, and her breath shook. “We have to be unanimous.”

Silas barked something that almost became a laugh and failed. “Unanimous. Great. Like it’s a vote.” He raked his free hand through his hair, tugging at the roots. “I can’t—” His voice cracked, and he looked away again. “I can’t do it.”

Mara didn’t move. “Then you don’t.”

Silas’s head snapped up. “Mara—”

She met his eyes. In her face was every night she’d stayed awake while the others slept. Every decision she’d made that the others didn’t have to hold. “He’s not going to turn while we negotiate our feelings.”

Jonah’s breath came a little faster. He pressed his back into the desk as if bracing himself against an invisible tide. “Mara,” he said, and there was a plea in it despite himself. “Don’t drag it out.”

Mara’s gaze softened, infinitesimally, and that softness made her look like she might crumble. “Do you want… do you want to say anything?”

Jonah swallowed. For a moment his stare went unfocused, as if he were searching for a door in the fog. “I want you to take my pack,” he said. “The little pocket on the inside—there’s a picture. Don’t—” He paused, blinking hard. “Don’t leave it for them.”

Leena nodded quickly, miserably, as if she could at least do that right.

“And,” Jonah continued, voice tightening, “don’t tell my sister anything if you ever find her. Not the details. Just… that I didn’t make you do it twice.”

Silas made a broken sound, a breath that wasn’t quite a sob.

Mara reached into her jacket and drew the pistol. She held it low, pointed at the floor. It looked absurdly small in her hand, a tool that could end a life and also never be enough.

The room seemed to pull inward around the metal, like the very air recognized its purpose.

“Jonah,” Mara said, and her voice was too quiet, because loud would feel like violence. “Are you sure?”

Jonah’s lips trembled. He pressed them together until they steadied.

Then he nodded, once. A single, final motion. Consent, given with the weight of everything he’d lived through.

“I’m scared,” he admitted, and the honesty of it hit them like a slap. “But I’m more scared of hurting you.”

Leena rose to her knees again, reaching for Jonah’s unbitten hand. She clasped it with both of hers, anchoring him as if she could keep him from drifting away. Her hands were cold. His were already too warm.

Silas stood rigid by the door, eyes fixed somewhere past Jonah, jaw clenched so tight the muscle jumped.

Mara shifted closer. Her breath rasped in her throat. She brought the pistol up, not with dramatic flourish but with the grim gentleness of someone lifting a blanket over a face.

Jonah looked at her, and there was a whole lifetime packed into the space between them—runs through ruined streets, whispered jokes in the dark, the trust of watching someone’s back when the world had no backs left to watch.

“Make it quick,” he said.

Mara’s eyes glistened. She blinked, and a tear slipped free anyway, tracing a line down the dirt on her cheek.

“I will,” she promised.

Leena squeezed Jonah’s hand hard enough to hurt, like pain could keep him here. “I’m here,” she whispered. “I’m here. I’m here.”

Jonah’s gaze flicked to her, and for a heartbeat his expression eased. “Thank you,” he breathed. His chest rose. Fell.

Mara steadied her grip with both hands.

Time did something strange—stretched, thinned, became a tight string pulled to breaking. In that suspended moment, the scrape outside seemed very far away. The ruined world held its breath.

The sound that followed was deafening in the small room, a hard punctuation that did not belong to anything living.

Jonah’s body jerked once and then went still. His hand remained in Leena’s grasp, suddenly heavier in a way weight had nothing to do with.

Mara stood frozen, arm extended, as if her muscles hadn’t received the message that it was over. Smoke curled faintly in front of her. Her ears rang, swallowing the silence into a dull roar.

Leena stared at Jonah’s face, waiting for him to inhale again, waiting for the tiny, ordinary motion that meant the world continued. Her grip loosened slowly, unwillingly, like prying fingers off a ledge.

Silas’s knees buckled, and he caught himself against the wall with his palm, breathing too fast. He didn’t look at the body. He didn’t look at Mara. He stared at the door, as if something might come through and make it all someone else’s fault.

Mara lowered the pistol at last. Her hand shook so hard she had to press her knuckles to her thigh to stop it.

She looked down at Jonah.

Not at the bite. Not at the blood. At the absence. The terrible cleanliness of it—the way a person could be there and then, in a single sound, not.

“I’m sorry,” she said, though Jonah couldn’t hear it.

Outside, the scraping resumed, drawn by the noise. The world, indifferent and hungry, remembered them.

Mara exhaled, a long, broken breath, and forced herself to move. She reached for Jonah’s pack with trembling fingers.

Leena flinched at the motion as though Mara were stealing him. Then she understood, and her face crumpled.

Silas finally turned his head. His eyes landed on Jonah’s stillness, and something in his expression shut down as if a door had slammed inside him.

Mara found the inner pocket, fingers clumsy. She pulled out the folded photograph and held it for a moment, not opening it, just feeling the paper. Proof that Jonah had belonged to a time with light in it.

“There’s no ceremony,” Mara said hoarsely, more to steady herself than to inform them. “We can’t stay.”

Leena nodded, wiping her face with the heel of her hand. “I’ll… I’ll carry his pack.”

Silas swallowed hard. “I’ll take point.”

Mara looked one last time at Jonah, committing the shape of him to memory before the world forced her to do what it always demanded: keep going.

Then she stood, stepped back, and left him there—not because it was easy, not because it was right, but because the alternative was letting the dead follow them wearing his face.

As they moved toward the door, the finality pressed against their ribs like a weight: that there would be no waking up from this. No fixing it. No undoing.

Only the echo of that one sound in a small room, and the empty space where Jonah’s future had been.

At first it doesn’t feel like madness. It feels like aftermath—like the way smoke clings to hair long after the fire is out. They expect panic, sirens, a pounding at the door. Instead there’s only the ordinary world, still intact, and that’s the first wrongness. The kettle still whistles. The sun still lays itself across the kitchen tiles. Their hands still know how to rinse a cup. The day keeps going as if nothing has changed, and that quiet becomes its own accusation.

The memory of it is sharp for a while, a bright shard they can’t stop touching with their mind. It has a beginning, middle, end—sequence, logic. They replay it to make sure it happened the way they remember, to check for loose ends. Each replay changes the shape of it: a different angle of the room, a different expression on the victim’s face, a different sound. The facts blur at the edges while the sensation stays vivid—heat, metallic taste, the wrong resistance of flesh. The brain, trying to protect itself, starts sanding down the details. That sanding is what scares them. Forgetting feels like getting away with it. Remembering feels like drowning.

Then the ghost arrives, not as a cinematic apparition but as a failure of perception.

It begins in the corner of their eye: a suggestion of someone standing where no one should stand. A vertical shape in the hallway. A pale patch by the coat rack. They turn, and there’s nothing. They look back, and the air looks thicker there, as if it’s holding the place open for a body that refuses to be absent.

They tell themselves it’s stress. Lack of sleep. The brain misfiring. That explanation should soothe them—should make it smaller, chemical, manageable—but it doesn’t. Because the “misfire” always looks like the same person. Always in their periphery. Never head-on. Like their guilt knows it can’t survive direct inspection, only the tremulous half-seeing where doubt breeds.

Sleep becomes a negotiation they keep losing. When they close their eyes, the room behind their eyelids is more populated than the one around them. They hear their own pulse and mistake it for footsteps. They wake up mid-breath, listening. In the dark, the furniture rearranges itself into silhouettes that might be shoulders, might be a face. Their mind starts treating shadows like evidence.

The second stage is not hallucination so much as contamination: everything becomes capable of reminding them.

A drain gurgles and it sounds like a throat trying to clear itself. A neighbor’s laugh punches a hole straight through their composure. A stain on a sidewalk becomes a lecture. The victim’s name appears in odd places—on a receipt, in a news ticker, in the mouth of a stranger who isn’t even saying it, just something close enough to make their stomach flip. Their attention becomes a magnet for the subject they’re trying not to touch. They stop watching movies because every plot feels like it’s angling toward their secret. They stop reading because every sentence feels like it could be about confession.

They begin to police themselves in public: smoothing their face into something neutral, tamping their reactions down so hard it takes effort to blink. They laugh half a second late. They answer questions with the wrong energy. They start to fear not the police but the ordinary gaze—the cashier, the coworker, the person waiting behind them at a crosswalk—because it feels like everyone has developed a new sense for rot.

The ghost starts to acquire behaviors. It is never simply present; it is positioned. Always where it can watch. Always where they have to decide whether to look. In mirrors it lingers a beat behind their reflection, as if the glass holds old footage. In the kitchen window at night, their own face overlays the dark outside, and behind it there’s a pale suggestion of another face, patient as mildew.

They begin to bargain with it in tiny, private ways.

*If I don’t look, it will go away.*
*If I count to ten.*
*If I wash my hands again.*

Washing becomes ritual. Scrubbing until the knuckles swell, until the skin is dry and papery. They buy stronger soap. They clean the grout with a toothbrush. Not because the house is dirty, but because the mind is trying to convert moral stain into something physical it can remove. The more they clean, the more they notice what can’t be cleaned: the invisible film on everything, the sensation that their life has a smell no one else comments on, some faint sweet-iron tang clinging to them like sweat.

Food turns to texture. Their mouth rejects certain consistencies—anything too soft, anything that yields. Meat becomes impossible. They chew mechanically and feel, grotesquely, how teeth meet resistance. Sometimes they swallow too quickly and gag, startled by their own body. Their body has become an accomplice they can’t trust.

They start speaking less, because words feel dangerous. A sentence is a path; a path might lead somewhere; somewhere might be the truth. When they do speak, they overcorrect. They become overly polite, overly agreeable, overly normal. They add little laugh-sounds in places laughter doesn’t belong. They apologize for things that don’t need apologies. Every interaction turns into a performance of innocence. The performance exhausts them, and exhaustion makes the edges of reality fray.

The ghost takes advantage of fatigue. It grows bolder when their defenses are down.

At the grocery store, a stranger’s shoulder in the aisle becomes the victim’s shoulder. For half a second their heart stops, and in that stop there’s a full, terrible certainty: *they’re here.* They step back so hard they bump into a display. The stranger turns, confused, and their face is wrong, wrong, wrong. Relief floods in alongside nausea. The ghost doesn’t need to be real to have power; it only needs to hijack the body’s alarm system. Their adrenal glands become loyal to the ghost.

Soon they can’t tell whether they’re seeing things or anticipating them. The periphery becomes a haunted region. Their eyes dart constantly, trying to catch the phantom in the act. This makes them look suspicious. This makes them more anxious. The cycle tightens like a wire.

There is a psychological rot that sets in when a person must live alongside a fact they refuse to integrate. The mind splits itself around it. One part insists: *It happened, and it is mine.* Another part insists: *It happened, and it is not mine.* They move through days with this internal argument humming under everything, like a refrigerator motor you can’t turn off. Every decision becomes complicated by the question of what kind of person makes such a decision. Even buying toothpaste feels loaded: *Do murderers prefer mint?* The brain becomes a courtroom that never adjourns.

Guilt doesn’t always look like remorse. Sometimes it looks like irritability, like contempt for other people’s small problems. Sometimes it looks like sudden tenderness that surprises them, misdirected kindness offered in a panic, like tossing coins into a well to appease something unseen. They donate to charities they don’t care about. They let strangers cut in line. They adopt rules: no stepping on cracks, no leaving dishes overnight, no music above a certain volume. Superstitions bloom because control is addictive when you’ve crossed a line that makes everything feel out of control.

Their imagination grows teeth. They start mapping consequences onto harmless details.

A siren in the distance: *They’re coming.*
A knock at a neighbor’s door: *It’s for me.*
A friend’s casual question: *They know.*

Even when no one is accusing them, they feel accused. Their mind turns every neutral stimulus into indictment. This is the rot: not the ghost itself, but the interpretive lens that becomes permanently warped. Reality is no longer neutral; it is coded.

The victim’s ghost becomes, in time, less like a figure and more like a climate. A pressure system that moves with them.

Sometimes it’s only a chill at the back of the neck when they pass certain places. Sometimes it’s the conviction that someone is standing behind them when they’re alone in a room. They stop sitting with their back to open space. They rearrange furniture. They keep lights on. They startle at their own reflection. Their home, which should be a refuge, becomes a maze designed by their own fear.

They begin to distrust their memories of who they were before. The “before” feels like a story someone told them. They try to access the old self—favorite songs, old photos—but each attempt feels like pressing on a bruise. The photos look staged, like evidence in a case file. The smile doesn’t fit. The eyes look like someone playing a role. They start to believe they were always this, that the murder didn’t change them so much as reveal them. That belief is a poison, because it makes redemption feel impossible, and when redemption feels impossible, the future shrinks to a corridor with no doors.

The ghost is patient. It doesn’t need to shout. It can wait until the moment their guard slips—when they’re brushing their teeth, when they’re driving on an empty road, when they’re half-asleep and the mind is most honest.

Then it appears in the corner again. A still shape. A head tilted in that unmistakable way. Not accusing, not pleading—simply present, as if saying: *I am the thing you did.*

They stop turning to look. Turning never helps. Looking directly at it only gives them the relief of emptiness and the immediate return of doubt: *What if it was there and I missed it? What if it moved? What if it’s learning?* Their eyes become trapped in the periphery, where certainty cannot exist. Their world becomes made of almosts.

And that’s how the madness settles in: not as a dramatic break, but as a gradual surrender of trust—in perception, in memory, in the solidity of the self. The murder is one act. The aftermath is the daily act of carrying it without letting it touch anything, and in trying not to stain the world, they stain their own mind. The ghost doesn’t have to be real. It only has to be inevitable.

The snow gives under their boots with a dull, exhausted crunch, each step heavier than the last. Breath rasps in their throat, and the world has narrowed to white ground, gray trees, and the ring of moving shadows that won’t stop tightening. When they finally back into the drifted bank and have nowhere left to go, the cold is everywhere at once—seeping through seams, stiffening fingers, making every heartbeat feel sluggish and far away.

The first bite doesn’t arrive like a clean, cinematic strike. It’s sudden weight and shock: a blunt impact that turns into pressure, then a tearing pain that blooms too fast to name. For a half-second their mind tries to make it abstract—an object, a trap—until the heat of it tells the truth. The wolf’s jaws clamp and the world jolts sideways, their body yanked off balance, the snow scraping their cheek as they go down.

Cold and heat collide in the same instant. The air is so sharp it feels like it’s cutting the inside of their nose; the snow against the wound is an immediate, stinging numbness, like plunging bare skin into ice water. But beneath that, the bite burns—an intense, living heat that pulses outward with each frantic beat of the heart. Blood is warm in a way that feels wrong in the winter: thick, slippery warmth spreading under clothing, steaming faintly before the cold steals it, turning it tacky, then chilling at the edges until it aches.

They can feel the contrast more clearly than the pain at first—the way the cold tries to hush everything, to make the limb distant and unreal, while the hot spill of blood insists on the body’s presence, on panic and life. The cold bites from the outside in; the injury flares from the inside out. For a moment it’s like being held between two kinds of teeth—winter’s numbing grip and the wolf’s brutal, immediate certainty.

Kestrel Vale didn’t run bounties for the romance of it. She ran them because the city above the clouds—Tier Nine, all glass ribs and neon arteries—paid well for problems that refused to stay solved.

Tonight’s problem was Juno Marr, a data-mule with a habit of stealing memories out of corporate skull-vaults and selling them back to the highest bidder. The contract tagged Marr as “noncompliant, high flight-risk,” which was executive code for: expect a chase, expect tricks, and expect the person you’re chasing to look you in the eye while lying.

Kestrel found her in the service underways beneath a commuter spine, where the air smelled of ozone from the mag-rails and old coolant. Marr was smaller than the dossier photo, hair shaved close, cheeks hollow from too many nights awake. She was crouched beside an access panel, fingers dancing in a spill of wire.

“You’re late,” Marr said without turning.

“I’m punctual,” Kestrel replied, stepping out of the shadow. “You’re early.”

Marr pivoted, and something sleek flashed in her hand—an injector pistol, illegal on this tier. The muzzle lifted toward Kestrel’s chest.

Kestrel didn’t shoot. She didn’t need to. Her glove was already talking to the stunner holstered along her forearm, waking it from sleep, charging its capacitors with a soft, mosquito-like whine only she could hear through her bone-conduction implant.

“Contract says intact,” she said. “Don’t make this messy.”

Marr’s smile was a blade. “You people always say that.”

The injector hissed. A dart snapped across the gap.

Kestrel snapped her wrist and let the dart thunk into the composite bracer meant for exactly this kind of negotiation. The impact barely registered. Marr’s eyes widened a fraction—just enough for Kestrel to close the distance.

Marr moved fast, twisting away, boots skidding on the damp metal grating. She struck at Kestrel’s throat with the pistol, then ducked and drove an elbow toward Kestrel’s ribs, trying to make space, trying to reach the access hatch behind her.

Kestrel caught the elbow, turned with it, and felt the tug of Marr’s strength—panic turning muscle into a lever. Marr wrenched free and bolted toward the hatch.

“No,” Kestrel said, and brought her arm up.

The stunner unfolded with a mechanical click, two prongs telescoping out like a mantis’s forelimbs. She aimed for the center mass—where the suit’s sensors could read impedance and the weapon’s governor could decide how hard to bite.

Marr spun at the last second, raising the injector like a talisman. Kestrel fired anyway.

The prongs kissed Marr’s jacket with a sharp crack, and the air between them snapped blue-white for an instant, like a miniature storm.

Marr’s body reacted before her mind could.

Every voluntary motion cut out, replaced by involuntary electrical bookkeeping: muscles obeying current instead of intention. results.model_response:
Cold metal kisses the back of their skull before they’re fully awake.

For a moment the world is only sensation: the granular itch of concrete dust on their cheek, a sour chemical tang in the air, the slow, deliberate pulse of something timed—an electronic tick that seems to echo inside their teeth. When they open their eyes, the ceiling is too close, stained and pocked, and the light above them is a single harsh bulb that makes every shadow look like a bruise.

They try to sit up and can’t.

Restraints bite their wrists and forearms, broad bands of leather cinched tight enough to turn panic into geometry. Their ankles are locked. Their torso is pinned by a bar that doesn’t allow much more than shallow breaths. When they test it again—harder, angry—something in the mechanism answers with a dry, mechanical click, as if acknowledging their effort and denying it at the same time.

The room is small. Intentionally so. Nothing to look at except the apparatus built around them, and the thing placed within reach like a cruel gift.

A tool. Too clean for this place. Too purposeful to be there by accident.

Their mind races ahead, trying to write a different story. Kidnapping, ransom, misunderstanding—anything but what the scene keeps insisting on. They search for an explanation in the details, because details feel like control. The worn grooves on a hinge. The pattern of bolts. A smear of old rust that says this has been used before.

That last thought lands like a weight.

A screen, mounted at the edge of their vision, flickers. The blue-white glow paints their hands a sickly color. A distorted voice crackles from a speaker, calm as an instruction manual, and the words arrive with the casual cruelty of someone reading the weather.

A choice framed as a lesson.
A countdown framed as mercy.
A way out that demands a piece of them.

They listen once, twice, as if repetition will change the meaning. The message ends and the timer begins in earnest, its numbers bright and indifferent.

Their throat goes dry. Their tongue feels too big for their mouth.

“No,” they say aloud, to the room, to the unseen watcher, to the idea that pain could be currency. The word sounds small against the ticking.

They jerk their hands again, testing the straps until their skin warms and then stings. The restraints hold. The mechanism answers with another click, and this time it’s followed by a soft whir somewhere behind the wall—something priming, or being reminded that it will have to do its job if they don’t do it first.

The psychological conflict doesn’t arrive as a single wave. It comes in layers.

First, disbelief: *This can’t be real.*
Then bargaining: *There has to be another latch. A loophole. A trick.*
Then a thin, rising horror as they realize the room has been designed by someone who anticipated bargaining.

They scan for alternatives. Their eyes snag on seams in the concrete, a vent cover, the edge of the screen. Nothing loose. No reassuring vulnerability. Their gaze keeps returning to the tool, to the part of the apparatus it clearly corresponds with, as if looking away might erase the relationship between them.

They feel their heart battering against the restraint bar. They count breaths to slow it down and fail; adrenaline doesn’t care about counting.

In their head, two voices begin to argue.

One is raw instinct, shrill and insistent: *Get out. Now. Do whatever it takes.*
The other is the part of them that still believes in lines you do not cross: *Not like this. Not by hurting yourself. Not for him.*

It’s a moral argument conducted in a body that is already flinching.

They imagine the pain in flashes—quick, involuntary pictures that turn their stomach. Their mind tries to outsource the act to someone else: a doctor, an accident, anything but their own hand. Because making the decision is somehow worse than the injury itself. Choice is what the trap is really taking.

They swallow and taste metal though there’s no blood yet.

The timer continues, steady as a metronome. Each second is a small shove.

They force themselves to look away from the numbers and down at their hands. Their fingers are trembling—fine motor tremors, the kind you can’t command into stillness. They flex them slowly, once, twice, feeling the stiffness where the straps compress tendon and bone. They press their palms against the leather, testing where it gives and where it doesn’t, mapping the limitations of their own body the way you map a room in the dark.

They do the same with their breathing. In through the nose—shallow. Out through the mouth—shaky. Again. Again. Preparation, not for bravery, but for function. If they are going to do anything at all, they have to be able to aim their mind as well as their hand.

The tool is within reach if they extend their arm to its limit. Just barely. That is not an accident. Nothing in this room is an accident.

They inch their hand toward it. Their shoulder protests against the restraint. The leather creaks. Their fingertips brush cold metal and they jerk back as though it burned them.

A laugh threatens to surface—hysterical, disbelieving. They clamp their jaw and it becomes a sob instead, swallowed hard.

*This is what he wants,* the rational voice says, more exhausted now than defiant. *To make it your fault. To make you participate.*

The instinct voice counters: *He already did. The moment you woke up here.*

That thought is the cruelest. It feels true.

They reach again, slower. Not because they’re calm, but because speed feels like surrender. Their fingers close around the handle. It’s heavier than they expect. Real. Its weight drags their wrist down and the strap bites tighter, as if punishing them for holding it.

They bring it closer, as close as the restraints allow, and just sit with it for a beat—an object that has become a question.

Their mouth moves without sound at first: *I can’t. I can. I can’t.*

They picture their own body as something separate, a machine that can be repaired later. They try to turn themselves into a stranger so it will hurt less to do what’s required. But the warmth of their skin, the living pulse under their thumb, keeps insisting on ownership.

The room amplifies everything: the rasp of their breathing, the squeak of leather, the tiny tremor in the tool’s metal as their grip shakes. They become hyperaware of sensations they usually ignore—the tackiness of sweat in their palm, the ache in their shoulder, the way fear makes the edges of vision sharpen while the center blurs.

They force their breathing into a rhythm again. In. Out. In. Out. They count. Not to be brave, but to stay present. Dissociation feels like slipping; slipping feels like losing the last thing they can still call theirs.

Their eyes flick to the timer. The numbers have crawled closer to the end.

The instinct voice grows louder, less articulate: *Now. Now. Now.*

The rational voice, cornered, makes its final argument not in ideals but in arithmetic: *If you don’t do it, something worse happens. If you do it, you might live. Living is the only way you ever get to make this right.*

That’s what breaks them—not the fear of pain, but the possibility that refusing could be a kind of pride they won’t survive.

They set their jaw until it aches. They adjust their grip, searching for steadiness. They plant their shoulder as best they can against the restraint bar to create leverage, to make their arm less of a trembling pendulum. Their free hand clenches into a fist so tight their nails leave crescents in their palm—an anchor, a distraction, a way to feel pain they chose instead of pain demanded.

They bring the tool into position. Their whole body fights it, not with strength but with revulsion, like trying to force a magnet against its match.

A sob escapes them, sharp and sudden, and they hate that it sounds like pleading.

“No one gets to make me,” they whisper, even as their hands hover, even as they prepare. The contradiction tastes like ash.

They close their eyes for half a second—half a second to remember daylight, to remember their own name, to remember that they were a person before they were a problem to be solved. When they open them again, there is no revelation, no courage descending from the ceiling. There is only the ticking and the choice and the terrible fact of their own will.

They inhale. Hold. Exhale.

Their grip steadies—not because the fear has left, but because it has nowhere else to go.

And with the timer glaring down its last indifferent seconds, they commit to the act the trap has demanded, moving with the careful, deliberate precision of someone trying to survive without letting the room take anything more than it already has.

The deck of the *Sea Wraith* rolled under a low, sullen sky, every plank slick with salt spray and the day’s earlier rain. The crew had gathered in a loose half-circle, boots braced wide as the ship climbed and fell, eyes fixed not on the horizon but on the man forced to his knees near the mainmast.

Ronan Hale—once a topman, once a loud mouth with louder dreams—kept his hands up as if he could hold the whole scene back with his palms. Rope bit into his wrists. His cheeks were pale in stark contrast to the bruised, windburnt skin of the men around him.

Captain Marrow stood before him like a figure carved from the ship itself: coat heavy with damp, black hair tied back, a thin line of scar cutting one eyebrow in two. He didn’t raise his voice. He didn’t need to.

“You thought to take my ship,” Marrow said, each word steady despite the ship’s sway. “You thought I’d wake with a knife at my throat and thank you for it.”

Ronan swallowed hard. His eyes darted from face to face, searching for something—pity, regret, a crack in the resolve of the crew. He found only hardened expressions and the tight, uncomfortable silence of men who had made their choice and now wanted the moment over.

“It was talk,” Ronan rasped. “Just talk. I—Captain, I never—”

“Aye,” Marrow said, tilting his head slightly, as if considering the weather. “And it’ll be talk that gets you killed. A poison in the cask spreads, if you don’t pour it out.”

He turned his gaze toward the bow where the plank had been laid out—an extra length of timber slid from the rail like a tongue, its end hanging over open water. Two crewmen dragged Ronan upright and marched him forward. The mutineer’s boots scraped, toes skidding as he tried to dig in. The effort was useless; the deck itself seemed to conspire against him, slick and unsteady.

Ronan’s breathing grew loud. Ragged. Too fast. The closer they came, the more his body betrayed him: his shoulders hunched as if bracing for a blow, his knees trembling as if they could buckle at any moment.

The sea below was an ugly green-blue, chopped into restless facets by the wind. It should have looked empty from this height—just waves, foam, and depth.

It didn’t.

Shadows moved beneath the surface in slow, deliberate arcs. At first it was only a suggestion, a dark crescent appearing and vanishing as the ship passed. Then another. Then two at once, sliding like knives through cloth, pacing the hull with patient hunger. Every time a wave peaked and thinned, the shapes sharpened—broad backs, a flick of tail, the pale flash of a belly rolling under.

The sharks had learned the ship’s habits. They followed not with frenzy, but with certainty, as if the ocean itself had begun to expect tribute.

Ronan saw them. His eyes widened until the whites showed all around, and his throat bobbed with a swallow that didn’t seem to go down. He tried to lean away from the rail, but the men at his arms held him firm.

“No,” he whispered, the word snatched thin by the wind. “No, please. Captain—Marrow—please.”

Captain Marrow stepped close enough that Ronan could smell the tar on his coat and the faint, sharp bite of rum.

“You asked the sea to choose between us,” Marrow said quietly. “Now it has.”

He lifted his voice just enough for the crew to hear.

“Let him look,” he commanded. “Let him understand what waits for those who’d put hands on the wheel.”

They forced Ronan to the very edge. The plank jutted out ahead, dipping slightly with the ship’s motion. Water hissed and slapped against the hull below, the sound hollow and hungry. Far beneath, one shark turned on its side and cut upward, its dorsal fin slicing the surface for a moment before it sank again—an unspoken promise.

Ronan’s fear became physical. It shook him, from his bound wrists to the soles of his boots. Tears mingled with sea spray on his face, and he blinked hard, frantic, as if he could clear the sight from his eyes.

Marrow’s expression didn’t change. “Forward.”

He stared down between each step, unable not to, as if the sea were pulling at his eyes. The sharks below circled in widening loops, dark commas in the water, gathering under the plank’s end. One passed directly beneath, close enough that Ronan could see the shape of its head, the blunt snout cutting through a patch of clearer water.

A wave rolled and lifted the surface. For a heartbeat, the sea smoothed, and the shadows aligned—three, maybe four—turning in concert, patient as a clock.

Ronan stopped halfway along, body rigid, heels planted. The plank dipped slightly with his hesitation.

“I can’t,” he choked out.

Behind him, the deck creaked as Captain Marrow stepped onto the plank’s base, not out of necessity but to make certain Ronan felt the pressure of command at his back. The captain’s boots were steady. Unhurried.

“You can,” Marrow said. “Or you’ll be helped.”

Ronan’s head jerked as if he’d been struck. His breath came in sharp bursts now, the kind that left him lightheaded. He tried to turn, but the narrowness of the plank and the pull of open air made him sway. His bound hands flailed slightly for balance, rope limiting him to awkward motions.

Below, the sea kept moving. The sharks kept circling. Occasionally a fin split the surface and vanished again, as calm and sure as a sail being trimmed.

“Last step’s the easiest,” someone called out, voice rough with forced humor. “Just don’t look down.”

Ronan looked down anyway. He couldn’t help it. Terror owned his eyes.

The end of the plank was only two paces away. Beyond it was nothing—only wind and water and those dark, waiting shapes.

He took one more step. Then another. The plank creaked, and the ship rolled, and Ronan’s balance wavered. He teetered at the very end, toes curled over the edge, chest heaving, a man on the lip of his own undoing.

Captain Marrow’s voice came one final time, quiet enough that it felt meant for Ronan alone.

“Go on,” he said. “Make peace with what you chose.”

Ronan’s face crumpled. A sound escaped him—half sob, half strangled prayer—and for a second he stood frozen between two worlds: the hard certainty of the deck behind him and the living hunger below.

Then his weight shifted, whether by trembling legs or the ship’s roll, and the ocean rose up to meet him.

Their fingers find it before their eyes do.

A hard, unfamiliar rectangle presses against their sternum under the fabric, too flat to be a phone, too heavy to be nothing. When they drag the shirt away from their skin, the air hits sweat-slick chest and the strap bites in response—nylon webbing pulled tight enough to leave pale furrows, tight enough that breathing turns into a negotiation. The device sits there with obscene calm, centered like a badge, the edges squared and unapologetic against the soft give of ribs.

The first wire catches their fingertip like a thorn.

It’s not smooth; it has that rubbery sheath that grips skin, that drags instead of gliding. Their nail slides along it and squeaks faintly, a tiny complaint. Another wire crosses it, and another—colors that don’t mean anything to them except *wrong*, a small tangle pinned down with tape that has gone slightly warm, slightly tacky. The tape lifts a fraction when they touch it, a whispery peel that makes their stomach flip. Underneath, the bundle has no give. It doesn’t flex the way a harmless object does. It feels deliberate.

Then the sound arrives, not as a dramatic countdown but as something intimate, something that’s been happening the whole time and only now has permission to be heard.

Tick.

It’s thin, mechanical, and too close. Not coming from the room—coming from *them*. The vibration is so subtle they think they imagine it, until they press their palm over the device and feel the faint, regular tremor against the heel of their hand, like a second heartbeat that doesn’t belong.

Tick.

Their own pulse throws itself against their throat, swelling there, frantic and wet. They try to inhale and the strap refuses to move. The breath catches, shallow and scraping, and it makes the wires shift a millimeter, which feels like moving a sleeping animal’s whiskers. Their fingertips go numb and oversensitive at once—every contact both distant and intolerably sharp.

Tick.

They freeze, and the freezing doesn’t help. It only makes them aware of everything else: the sweat cooling at the edges, the hair on their chest pinned beneath adhesive, the way the plastic casing digs harder when they hunch as if they can fold away from it. Their tongue sticks to the roof of their mouth. Saliva tastes metallic, like coins.

They want to pull it off. Their hands twitch toward the straps, seize a handful of webbing, and stop as if burned. The strap feels rough, woven, indifferent; it rasps their knuckles, and in that rasp is the sudden, irrational certainty that *any* friction might be enough. Their mind starts making pictures without permission—sparks, shrapnel, a red blur—each one a flashbulb behind their eyes.

Tick.

They listen harder, trying to count, trying to find a pattern that will be a rule they can obey. The ticks don’t care about their attention. They keep coming at the same merciless pace, neither hurrying for their panic nor slowing for their pleading. Every interval feels shorter than the last. Their thoughts trip over themselves: *Don’t move. Move. Get help. Don’t breathe. Breathe.*

Tick.

A laugh threatens to spill out—high and strangled, disbelieving—and it catches halfway, turning into a choked sound that makes them hate their own throat. Their hands hover in the air, shaking, fingers splayed like they can hold the world away by not touching it. When they do touch again, it’s barely, the soft pad of a finger laid against a wire as if it might soothe it.

The wire is cold. The casing is warm. Their skin is hot. Nothing matches.

Tick.

The hysteria rises like water behind a door. It presses against their ribs. It makes their vision narrow, edges tunneling, the room pulling away. Small sounds become enormous: the rustle of their shirt, the rasp of breath, the tick drilling straight into the center of their skull. Their brain starts chanting in a raw, childish loop—*no, no, no*—as if repetition might build a wall.

Tick.

Their heart hammers so hard it feels like it could jostle the device. That thought is a hook in their stomach. They clamp an arm across their chest, not to hold it in place but to hold themselves together, nails digging crescents into their own skin through fabric. They can feel the device through every layer: the unforgiving corners, the tight straps, the trapped wires under tape, the faintest quiver of the mechanism doing its patient work.

Tick.

There’s nowhere in their body left to put the fear. It spills outward into trembling limbs, into a throat that can’t decide between screaming and silence, into eyes that sting because blinking feels like time passing. They stand there with an explosive strapped to their chest and the sound inside them is the ticking and the blood and the mounting, unbearable knowledge that their life has been turned into something measurable.

The house had the wrong kind of quiet—the kind that didn’t feel empty so much as held. Air pressed against the back of Rowan’s throat when they stepped inside, the front door clicking shut behind them with a soft, final sound.

They stood still in the narrow entryway, listening.

Nothing. No refrigerator hum, no distant pipes, no neighbor’s TV bleeding through the walls. Just the faint tick of the hallway clock, measured and patient.

Rowan’s fingers found the light switch by habit and snapped it up.

Nothing happened.

They clicked it down, up again. A dull plastic tap, a dry internal click. The darkness stayed.

“Okay,” Rowan breathed, too quiet to be for anyone else. The word came out thin. Their phone screen lit their palm in a harsh white rectangle, throwing the shadow of their hand across the wallpaper in a warped shape.

2%.

Of course.

They lifted the phone higher, the beam skimming along the hall: coat hooks, the umbrella stand, the framed photo of them laughing on the beach—faces bright in a way that suddenly felt like it belonged to someone else. The light made everything look flattened, edges too sharp, corners too deep.

Rowan’s shoes scuffed the runner rug as they took one careful step forward, then another. The floorboards complained in a long, drawn-out creak that seemed to travel ahead of them, announcing their presence room by room.

Rowan stopped. Held their breath.

The creak died, leaving a ringing silence.

Somewhere deeper in the house, something made a faint sound—soft enough it could have been the house settling. Soft enough it could have been nothing at all.

Rowan swallowed. The motion felt loud.

They moved again, slower now, phone light angled down at their feet like it could keep the dark from touching them. Their free hand reached out and brushed the wall, fingertips skimming the paint to keep their bearings. The hallway narrowed in their mind, the darkness thickening at the far end where the living room opened up.

The clock ticked behind them like a metronome. Each beat sounded more deliberate than the last.

Rowan’s phone buzzed once—no notification, just the desperate tremor of a dying battery. The screen dimmed for a heartbeat and Rowan’s stomach tightened. They thumbed it back brighter, the light flaring, catching dust motes drifting like slow, pale insects.

They made it to the archway and paused, peering into the living room.

Furniture crouched in low shapes: the couch, the coffee table, the bookshelf. The curtains over the front window were drawn, but a thin strip of streetlight slipped through a gap and cut a faint silver line along the floor.

Rowan’s gaze snagged on something out of place.

A corner of the curtain near the window wasn’t hanging right. Not torn—just… disturbed, as if someone had brushed past it. A subtle difference Rowan would have missed if their heart hadn’t already been hammering for a reason they couldn’t name.

“Did I…” Rowan whispered, then stopped. The sound of their own voice in the room felt like a mistake.

They stepped into the living room. The floorboard under their left foot gave a sharp crack. Rowan flinched, lifting their foot as if the sound could bite.

In the dark at the edge of the room, near the doorway to the kitchen, a shadow shifted—not a broad movement, just a slight adjustment, like a person shifting their weight. It could have been the trick of Rowan’s weak phone light, the beam wobbling with their hand.

Rowan froze. The phone’s light steadied, sweeping the space in a slow arc.

Couch arm. Empty chair. The glass front of the cabinet reflecting the phone screen back in a tiny, trembling square. Nothing else.

Rowan’s lungs burned. They forced themselves to breathe through their nose, slow. The air smelled faintly of something metallic under the usual scent of laundry detergent and old wood.

They turned toward the kitchen. The doorway yawned black. The phone light reached only a few feet in, catching the edge of the counter and the dull shine of the sink.

Then—there. A glint, a hard, quick spark near the corner of the doorway.

Rowan’s light shifted a fraction. The glint vanished.

Rowan’s fingers tightened around the phone until their knuckles ached. “Hello?” they called, louder than they meant to, as if volume could make the fear reasonable.

Silence answered. The clock continued to tick, now muffled by distance.

Rowan’s mind offered explanations in frantic succession: power outage, blown fuse, neighbor’s cat slipped in, something fell, you’re tired, you’re making it up. Their body did not listen. Their body cataloged the exit behind them, the dark hallway leading to the back door, the narrow route to the stairs.

They backed up one step, shoes whispering against the rug. Another.

The phone buzzed again, a last shaky warning. The screen dimmed, and Rowan jabbed at it with their thumb. A bar of red. 1%.

They stared at it, the little number suddenly more terrifying than any sound.

Somewhere in the kitchen, a faint scrape—metal against wood, subtle as a breath—ran along the edge of something. It was not loud. It was deliberate.

Rowan’s head snapped up.

The phone light flicked toward the sound, cutting across the kitchen entrance. For a moment it caught the sheen of a blade, half-hidden, the thin line of it reflecting like a narrow smile. The hand holding it remained in darkness, arm angled close to a body tucked behind the doorframe.

Rowan didn’t see a face. Didn’t need to.

They stepped back too fast and their heel caught the edge of the rug. Their balance went. The phone jerked, the beam skittering across ceiling, wall, floor—wild, useless—then they caught themselves against the bookshelf. A paperback slid out and thudded to the carpet.

The intruder didn’t rush. They didn’t speak. The only thing that moved was the knife, tilting slightly as if aligning to the shifting light.

Rowan’s phone screen flashed once, dimmer.

Then it went black.

Darkness slammed down, full and immediate. Rowan’s eyes widened, straining, but there was nothing to adjust to fast enough. The world reduced to sound and the thick pressure of their own pulse. In that instant the house felt enormous, every room a pocket of unseen space that could hide anything.

Nothing. No refrigerator hum, no distant pipes, no neighbor’s TV bleeding through the walls. Just the faint tick of the hallway clock, measured and patient.

Rowan’s fingers found the light switch by habit and snapped it up.

Nothing happened.

They clicked it down, up again. A dull plastic tap, a dry internal click. The darkness stayed.

2%.

Of course.

They lifted the phone higher, the beam skimming along the hall: coat hooks, the umbrella stand, the framed photo of them laughing on the beach—faces bright in a way that suddenly felt like it belonged to someone else. The light made everything look flattened, edges too sharp, corners too deep.

Rowan’s shoes scuffed the runner rug as they took one careful step forward, then another. The floorboards complained in a long, drawn-out creak that seemed to travel ahead of them, announcing their presence room by room.

results.model_response:
In the trench the air changes first—its weight, its taste. It doesn’t arrive like a blast so much as a creeping wrongness, a low fog that clings to sandbags and coats the back of the throat. The soldier inhales before he understands he shouldn’t, and the breath lands like a wet chemical burn.

His eyes sting and flood instantly, lids clamping shut on reflex. The skin around them feels scraped raw, as if rubbed with lye. The inside of his nose and mouth flare with a sharp, metallic bite; saliva surges, thick and sour, and he can’t swallow without pain. When he tries to shout a warning, the sound fractures into a rasp—his voice reduced to a harsh whisper, then nothing.

Breathing becomes work. The first coughs are short and involuntary, like a body trying to eject an intruder, but they quickly turn into deep, tearing spasms that bend him over. Each cough steals the air he was trying to pull in, leaving him in a cruel loop: inhale, burn; cough, empty; reach again. His chest tightens as if a strap has been cinched around his ribs. He tries to draw a full breath and can’t—only shallow sips that never reach the bottom of his lungs. The muscles in his neck stand out as he gulps for air, and his shoulders hunch, desperate to open space that isn’t there.

As the irritation deepens, the airway feels swollen and narrow. The air that does get through comes with a high, strained sound, and it feels colder than it should—like breathing over glass. Mucus thickens; the throat feels coated, sticky, obstructed. He spits and coughs reflexively, trying to clear it, but the act only inflames everything further. His lips tingle and then go numb; the edges of the world blur behind tears and the haze hugging the trench floor.

The physical struggle drags his mind into panic. His thoughts stop being tactical and become animal-simple: *air, air, air.* Time distorts into sharp snapshots—someone’s gloved hands yanking at a mask strap, the slick wood of a rifle stock under trembling fingers, the black mouth of the dugout that suddenly looks too far away. He can’t track orders. Words from others arrive muffled, as if through water, and he can’t tell whether he’s hearing them or imagining them.

Fear turns to a jittering, angry urgency. He claws at his own collar or mask because the brain mislabels the sensation—*something is choking me*—and wants to tear it away, even when doing so makes it worse. The body shakes with adrenaline; hands fumble and slip. He tastes bile from retching between coughs. He’s aware, in an abstract, humiliating way, that he might be drooling, that he can’t control it, but there’s no room for dignity—only the relentless accounting of breath.

If the exposure continues, exhaustion sets in fast. The coughing becomes weaker but no less frequent, each one a blunt punch to the ribs. The soldier’s face can take on a dusky, mottled look as oxygen runs short; his pulse pounds in his ears. He tries to focus on a single task—*get the mask sealed, get higher ground, get out of the low pocket of the trench*—but his thinking keeps slipping, as if his mind is losing traction. Confusion edges in: simple actions feel complicated, and he has to force himself to remember which way to turn, where the ladder is, how to work his own fingers.

Even after he’s out of the densest cloud, the sensation doesn’t end cleanly. The throat still feels raw, the lungs irritated, as if he’s inhaled smoke and ground pepper. Each breath carries a faint sting, and every time he tries to draw in more air, his body braces—waiting for the burn to return. The fear lingers too, a trembling aftershock: the memory of not being able to breathe, of the air itself turning hostile, threaded through every shallow, careful inhale.
