Smoke seeps in first as a taste—bitter, oily, wrong—sliding across the tongue and clinging to the back of the throat like tar. It gathers low along the floorboards and then rises in rolling sheets, swallowing the room’s corners, softening the edges of everything familiar until even the doorway looks like a smudged sketch.

They suck in a breath out of reflex and instantly regret it.

The air burns on the way down, not like cold air on a winter run, but like swallowing something lit. Their lungs seize, confused and furious, coughing hard enough to wrench their ribs. Each hack drags more smoke in. Each inhale feels smaller than the last, as if the building is tightening around their chest.

Somewhere beyond the wall, fire crackles with a wet, hungry sound—wood giving up. The heat isn’t just *hot*; it’s pressure. It pushes against their face, against their eyelids, against their teeth. Sweat beads and then instantly turns slick, making their grip on the doorknob unreliable. The metal is already warming, radiating a warning through the skin.

“Come on,” they rasp, voice swallowed by the roar. The word comes out thin, sliced to pieces by coughing.

They lurch toward the door anyway, half-blind, hand stretched out like it can part the smoke. Their fingers find the knob. It feels like a coin pulled from a furnace. Pain snaps up their arm, sharp and immediate, and they jerk back with a strangled sound, shaking their hand as if that can fling the heat off.

The rival’s face flashes in their mind—too calm, too pleased—standing in the hallway earlier, a hand on their shoulder for just a second too long. A scent like gasoline. The soft click of a latch that shouldn’t have locked. The moment they realized they weren’t going to be *fighting* tonight, they were going to be *watched*.

Panic doesn’t arrive all at once. It stacks. It piles up in the ribs, in the throat, in the palms. It makes the room shrink. It makes time jagged.

They drop to their knees, trying to remember what they’ve heard: stay low, find clean air, follow the wall. Their hands sweep along baseboards, knuckles knocking against scattered debris—paper curling into black petals, a fallen picture frame, the leg of a chair that’s already smoldering. The smoke is thicker here, but the heat above is worse; it presses down like a heavy hand.

They crawl, choking, eyes watering so hard they can’t see. Tears streak sideways across their cheeks, instantly drying where the heat catches them. The back of their neck prickles; then it stings; then it feels like someone held a match too close. The air itself seems to scald.

Another breath. Another mistake. Their lungs flutter, trying to find a rhythm that isn’t there. The cough that follows is deep and ugly, dragging something raw up from inside. For a heartbeat the room tilts; sparks dance in their vision that have nothing to do with the flames.

A beam overhead groans.

They freeze, ears ringing, and listen—because listening is all they can do when the smoke takes their sight. The sound comes again: wood warping, nails complaining, a slow, tortured bend. Dust and ash sift down onto their hair and shoulders like filthy snow.

They scramble forward, nails catching on the floorboards, and their palm smears through something wet—water? No, too slick. They glance down and catch a faint rainbow sheen in the dim: spilled accelerant, feeding the fire, guiding it. A deliberate trail. A plan.

The realization lands heavier than the smoke.

They find a second door—closet, maybe, or a back room. Their fingers fumble for the handle. The heat off it is less murderous than the first. Hope—sharp, immediate—flares in their chest.

They yank.

It gives a fraction. Something on the other side resists, as if the door is shouldered shut. They throw their weight into it, coughing, legs slipping. The wood shudders. A crack of air snakes through the gap—cooler, cleaner.

Then the ceiling above them snaps like a gunshot, and the world erupts in a shower of embers.

They look up just as the burning beam begins to fall, and at the same moment the door finally swings inward—revealing a narrow, smoke-dark space and, at the far end of it, the faint outline of a window with pale light leaking around its frame—

—and they have no time to decide which way to throw themselves.

I can’t write a step-by-step, “cold calculated” assembly/prep sequence for a long‑range rifle intended to kill someone—that crosses into actionable guidance for real-world violence. I can, however, give you a hard‑boiled monologue that keeps the technical side abstract and focuses on mood, restraint, and the character’s moral rot.

---

Night has a way of turning everything honest.

In the daytime, people lie with their mouths. After dark, they lie with their lights—office windows burning late to look important, streetlamps humming like they’re keeping the city safe, neon promising warmth to anyone dumb enough to believe it. But out here, where the air tastes like old concrete and rain that never quite falls, there’s nothing to hide behind. Just angles. Distance. Consequence.

The case rests on the table like a coffin that hasn’t decided who it belongs to yet.

I open it slow. Not because I’m savoring anything—there’s nothing to savor—but because haste is how amateurs die and professionals end up on the news with their faces blurred. Inside, everything is where it should be. Clean. Quiet. Patient. Tools don’t judge you. They don’t ask why. They just wait for your hands to stop shaking, if they ever did.

Mine don’t.

That’s the part people get wrong when they tell stories about men like me. They think you have to be made of ice, like you’re born without the part that flinches. Truth is, the flinch never leaves. You just learn to fold it up small and keep it in a pocket you never reach into when the time comes.

I lay things out with the same care a priest might use with relics, if priests were honest about what they worship. Pieces. Components. Metal that catches the room’s dim light and gives it back without warmth. Fabric that won’t reflect. A small inventory of choices already made. The ritual isn’t holy, but it is precise.

The work is mostly checking.

Checking that nothing’s missing. Checking that nothing’s loose. Checking that what’s supposed to align does. You don’t force anything—you don’t argue with physics. You confirm. You verify. You let certainty accumulate in tiny, boring increments until the moment itself is nothing but a math problem with a heartbeat at the end of it.

That’s what frightens me, if I’m being honest in the way only a man alone can afford.

Not the blood. Not the scream that may or may not happen depending on distance and dumb luck. It’s how ordinary it feels to prepare. Like fixing a door that sticks. Like tying a tie. Like brushing lint off your coat before a date you don’t intend to enjoy.

People want morality to be a bright line, something you can see from far away. Good on this side, evil on that side. Easy.

My line is a smudge.

I’ve told myself every story that makes the mirror easier. That the target is worse than me. That the money is just money, and money is what the world runs on, and I’m only another cog. That I’m careful, so I’m merciful. That I’m distant, so I’m clean.

Distance doesn’t make you clean. It just makes you quiet.

I fit the pieces together without drama, because drama is for men who want to be remembered. I don’t. I tighten what needs tightening—no strain, no heroics—then I stop and look at my hands like they belong to someone else. They’re steady. They’re competent. They’re the hands of a man doing a job.

That’s the scariest part: competence.

There’s a moment in every job, right before it becomes inevitable, when you can still turn back. People think it’s when you take the money, or when you say yes on the phone, or when you climb the stairs. Those are just paperwork.

The real moment is here, in the room with the door closed, when you finish preparing and realize there’s nothing left to do but go. When the last check is done and you can’t pretend you’re still deciding. When the gear is ready and, by extension, so are you.

I pause, and in the pause, I hear the things I keep buried under routine.

Somebody’s going to have an empty chair tomorrow.

Somebody’s going to dial a number that won’t pick up. Somebody will blame themselves for not noticing a sign, as if death sends invitations. Somebody will hate a faceless stranger and be right to do it. And I’ll walk away with the same face I walked in with, which is its own kind of theft.

There are men who do this and tell themselves they’re predators. They like the title. It makes them feel big.

I’ve never been a predator. Predators kill to eat.

I kill because somebody pays me to.

That’s not strength. That’s a vacancy you can rent by the hour.

I close the case for a second, like a man might press a book shut to keep the words from crawling out. I breathe in. I breathe out. The air comes back the same. Nothing in the universe shifts to stop me. No cosmic hand reaches down to slap my wrist. That’s another lie people tell themselves—that the world corrects for evil. It doesn’t. It just keeps score in a language nobody reads until it’s too late.

I open the case again. Not because I want to, but because wanting doesn’t factor in. I take what I need and leave what I don’t. I don’t look at the empty spaces where everything used to sit. Empty spaces are invitations to think.

Outside, the city keeps pretending it’s safe.

Inside, I finish the last quiet checks, and I feel the weight of what I’m carrying settle in—not just in my hands, but somewhere deeper, where names should be. It’s always heavier there. That’s the part no case can hold, no solvent can clean, no distance can reduce.

I tell myself the same thing I always tell myself, the same thing that keeps my feet moving when my mind wants to sit down and stay.

It’s a job.

And then, because I’m not entirely dead yet, I add the truth underneath it, the one that never gets any easier no matter how many times you repeat it:

It’s a job that makes me less human every time I do it.

I latch the case. I kill the light. I step into the hall like a man stepping into his own sentence.

The real moment is here, in the room with the door closed, when you finish preparing and realize there’s nothing left to do but go. When the last check is done and you can’t pretend you’re still deciding. When the gear is ready and, by extension, so are you.

It’s a job.

It’s a job that makes me less human every time I do it.

Rainwater ran in thin, oily ribbons along the cracked concrete, turning the back alley into a dark mirror broken by trash and puddles. A flickering security light above a dented service door kept time like a nervous pulse—on, off, on—washing the brick in brief, sickly color and then dropping it back into shadow.

Marek got there first, hood up, shoulders tight, a plastic grocery bag clutched like it contained something fragile instead of contraband. He kept glancing at the mouth of the alley, as if the street might spit out a patrol car any second.

Juno arrived a minute later from the opposite end, moving fast but trying to look casual, boots splashing softly. Her breath fogged in the cold. She didn’t stop until she was an arm’s length away, close enough that Marek could smell cheap cigarettes and adrenaline.

“You got it?” she asked.

Marek lifted the bag a fraction, then lowered it again. “You got *my* half?”

Juno’s hand went into her jacket. Marek’s chin lifted, a reflexive flinch, because hands disappeared into pockets right before things went wrong. She pulled out a folded envelope—too thin. Marek’s eyes narrowed.

“That’s not enough,” he said.

“It’s what I have,” Juno snapped. “And it’s cash. Not promises.”

Marek’s laugh came out dry. “You said full. You said you had someone lined up.”

“I *did.* He backed out. Or he got spooked. Or he got picked up—does it matter?” Her voice climbed, then she clamped it down, glancing at the alley mouth. “We don’t have time to haggle.”

Marek shifted his weight, blocking the bag with his body. “No money, no—”

Juno stepped in, too close now, her gaze hardening. “Don’t do this.”

“I’m not doing anything,” Marek said. “You’re the one—”

He stopped because Juno’s hand came out again, not with cash this time but with a dull flash of metal. A short blade, more utility than weapon, but it caught the security light like a wink.

Marek froze for half a heartbeat—long enough for the cold to sharpen in his throat. Then he took a step back, palms lifting. “Put it away.”

Juno’s eyes were wet with exhaustion rather than tears. “I’m not leaving empty-handed.”

“You think I’m going to stab you?” Marek tried to laugh again and failed. “Jesus, Juno.”

“Don’t say my name like you know me,” she hissed, and the knife came up a little higher.

The air between them felt suddenly narrow, packed tight with the sound of their breathing. Marek looked past her once, instinctively, and that tiny shift of attention was enough.

Juno lunged.

It wasn’t clean or practiced. It was desperation turned into motion—shoulders forward, knife hand leading. Marek reacted like someone swatting away an insect that could kill him. He slapped at her wrist, caught her forearm, and shoved sideways. Their bodies collided with the damp brick, hard enough to knock the breath from Marek’s lungs.

The bag crinkled and slipped from his grip, thudding to the ground with a wet slap.

“Stop!” he grunted, wrestling for her knife hand. Juno twisted, teeth bared, and drove her weight into him. Her free hand clawed at his hoodie, trying to yank him off balance.

Marek’s fingers found her wrist. He squeezed, trying to numb her grip, but his hands were shaking and his skin was slick with rain. The knife handle shifted. The blade wavered between them, close enough that he could feel its coldness without it touching him.

Juno jerked her arm downward.

Marek tried to jump back, but his heel hit something—an unseen bottle or a broken chunk of concrete—and his foot skated. For a moment he was weightless, off-center.

The knife caught him.

Not a dramatic plunge, not a movie stab. More like a sudden, sharp interruption—an impact with a brief resistance, then a slide. It landed along his side, near the lower ribs, just beneath the edge of his jacket.

At first the sensation was almost confusingly small: a hot, bright sting like a snapped rubber band, so immediate it stole his voice. Then the pain deepened, blooming outward in a fast wave, turning from sting to burn to a thick, nauseating pressure. His body responded before his mind did—muscles clenching, breath hitching, stomach tightening as if trying to pull away from itself.

“Ah—” Marek gasped, and the sound came out thin.

The security light flicked off. In the dark, pain became its own illumination. He felt the knife being pulled back—its edge dragging like a line of fire under his skin—followed by a sudden coldness where the air hit the opening. The cold didn’t soothe; it made the hurt feel sharper, like the wound had teeth.

Juno made a sound that could have been a sob or a curse. “I didn’t—”

Marek’s hand slammed over his side, palm pressing instinctively. The contact sent a jolt through him, a deep ache that seemed to pulse in time with his heartbeat. With each beat, there was a subtle pushing sensation under his hand—his body insisting on the injury, making it impossible to ignore.

He shoved forward with his shoulder, using his weight to pin her knife arm against the wall. Juno struggled, breath ragged, her other hand pushing at his chest.

“Let go!” she cried.

Marek’s vision tunneled for a second, edges going gray. The alley tilted. He forced his eyes open wide, forced air into his lungs. Breathing hurt; every inhale tugged at the injured area, making it feel like something inside him had been snagged and was being pulled.

He found his voice through clenched teeth. “Drop it.”

Juno’s wrist trembled. The knife hovered, then clattered to the ground, metal ringing dully on concrete.

Marek didn’t relax. He couldn’t. He kept her pinned another second, longer than necessary, because the second he let go he was terrified his legs would fold. His hand stayed pressed to his side, warmth spreading under his palm, sticky and wrong.

The security light flicked on again, washing the alley in pale yellow. Juno stared at Marek’s hand, then up at his face. The bravado had drained out of her, leaving only shock and the hollow look of someone realizing the line they’d crossed.

“I—I didn’t mean—” she started.

Marek’s mouth worked. His tongue felt thick. His skin had gone clammy, sweat mixing with rain. The pain was no longer a single point; it radiated, a constant burn threaded with sharper spikes whenever he moved wrong, as if the injury had its own opinion about what he was allowed to do.

He forced himself to bend, slowly, keeping pressure with one hand as he reached for the bag with the other. The movement made the pain flare, a bright lance that made his stomach roll.

“Take it,” he rasped, shoving the bag toward her with a shaky arm. “Just—take it and go.”

Juno hesitated, eyes flicking toward the alley entrance again, toward the street and whatever consequences waited there. Then she snatched the bag, fingers fumbling.

Their eyes met once more: two desperate people suddenly aware that desperation had teeth, and it didn’t care who it bit.

Juno backed away, steps unsteady, then turned and ran, her footsteps fading into the rain-slick night.

Marek slid down the wall until he was sitting on the cold concrete. The brick pressed into his shoulder blades. He kept his hand clamped to his side, feeling the throb, the warmth, the trembling weakness spreading through his limbs. Each breath came shallow and careful, as if the air itself had turned dangerous.

Somewhere beyond the alley, a car passed, tires hissing on wet asphalt, indifferent as the security light above him continued its anxious blinking—on, off, on—marking the moments while Marek stared at his own shaking hand and tried not to panic at how quickly the world could tip.

Rain had been working the alley for hours, worrying at the brick like a tongue at a loose tooth. It pooled in the cracks of the pavement and ran in thin brown ribbons toward the storm drain, carrying cigarette ash and something darker that didn’t belong in water.

The patrol car’s lights washed the walls in slow red-blue bruises. The uniform at the mouth of the alley kept his shoulders square, trying not to look past me.

“Detective Kincaid,” he said, voice too loud for the tight space.

I ducked under the tape without answering. The air changed immediately—cooler, wetter, and thick with the metallic bite that cuts through exhaust and garbage like a straight razor. Blood has a smell even after rain tries to bargain with it. Wet pennies, warm meat, iron on the back of the throat.

My shoes found traction in grit and broken glass. Somewhere overhead a gutter dripped steady, patient. The alley was a narrow corridor between a shuttered bar and a tenement with windows like missing teeth. A dumpster sat halfway down, lid cocked open, its breath sour with rot. The victim lay beyond it, where the alley pinched toward a back gate chained shut.

The body wasn’t posed. It had been dropped. One arm reached out as if for the gate, fingers bent and stiffening around nothing. The other was tucked under the torso at a wrong angle, elbow turned in a way elbows aren’t supposed to turn. Rain had slicked the skin and plastered hair to the forehead. The face was turned toward the wall, cheek pressed into damp concrete, and the streetlight caught the glossy sheen of what had leaked out and spread.

I stopped a pace away. Close enough to read, far enough not to step on words.

No theatrics. No prayer. Just inventory.

Male. Mid-thirties, maybe. Clothes cheap but clean once. Dark jacket soaked through, fabric darker where it clung to the ribs. A shoe missing. The remaining shoe’s sole had a fresh scrape as if he’d been dragged over something sharp. His pockets were turned out, lining bunched and shining with rainwater. Robbery, or someone making it look like robbery. Both smelled the same from here.

I crouched, careful with the angle of my knees so I wouldn’t touch anything I couldn’t account for later. The cold seeped through my trousers immediately, alley chill making its way into bone like it had a key.

There were marks on the neck—deep, ugly bruising already blooming under the skin, the color of old plums. Finger-shaped. It told a story of hands and panic, of air denied. Below that, the collar was torn. Buttons popped and lost in the dark.

The violence wasn’t just in the wounds. It was in the way the body had been handled afterward. The way the head had bounced against the wall hard enough to leave a smear—thin, diluted by rain, but unmistakable. The wall held it like a confession.

I took out my notepad. The pen was cold enough to sting my fingers.

“Photographer?” I called without turning.

“On the way,” someone answered from behind the tape. The voice sounded young. I didn’t bother learning it.

I scanned the ground in a widening circle. Cigarette butts, flattened and waterlogged. A bottle cap. A torn fast-food wrapper that clung to a puddle like it didn’t want to be carried away. Near the victim’s outstretched hand, half-hidden under the glare of a streetlight and the muddied sheen of rain, something pale glinted.

I leaned in, eyes doing the work my hands didn’t need to do yet. A fingernail. Not his. Too small, painted a chipped red. Someone had fought close enough to leave pieces behind. The alley kept souvenirs.

The smell of bleach drifted faintly under everything, thin and dishonest. Somebody had tried to clean, or at least to change the flavor of the air. It didn’t work. It never did. Blood doesn’t negotiate.

My gaze moved to the gate. The chain was new, bright steel against old rust. The padlock looked like it had been recently handled, fingerprints waiting in the moisture. On the ground beneath it, scuffed mud showed a hasty turn, heel marks overlapping, as if someone had hesitated and then decided not to go through.

I stood, slow. My joints complained in the cold, the kind of complaint that comes from too many nights like this. I didn’t let it reach my face.

There was a sound behind me—the faint, wet crunch of a boot on gravel. The medical examiner approached, hunched against the drizzle, kit in hand. Her eyes went straight to the body and didn’t flinch.

“Morning,” she said.

“It’s not,” I said, and flipped to a clean page.

She knelt beside the victim with the practiced care of someone working on a machine they’d repaired too often. She didn’t touch him yet, just looked. Her flashlight traced the bruising, the torn collar, the angle of the arm.

“Strangulation?” I asked.

“Likely,” she said. “And blunt force. See the swelling at the temple. He hit something hard. Wall, maybe. Ground. Could be both.”

The rain tapped the dumpster lid, a soft, impatient drumming. Somewhere a siren rose and faded, never coming closer. The city kept moving. It always kept moving.

I wrote: *Ligature? No visible. Manual? Bruising suggests. Blunt trauma.* The words sat in the notebook like they meant something solid. They were the closest thing to control.

My eyes went back to the victim’s hand. The fingers had dirt under the nails. Not alley dirt—lighter, sandy. Construction site, maybe. Or a park. It was a small detail, but small details were often the only honest ones.

“Any ID?” the uniform called from up the alley.

“Not yet,” I said.

I knew the routine. Bag the hands. Photograph every angle. Mark the evidence. Build a timeline from what water hadn’t washed away and what people would lie about later. There was a kind of comfort in procedure, if you could call it that—a rail to hold onto in a place where someone had died badly and the world expected you to make it make sense.

I stepped around the body, careful of the puddles that weren’t just puddles. Near the wall, under the smear, a faint print darkened the brick—a handprint, fingers spread, as if whoever did this had steadied themselves while they worked. The rain had softened it, but not erased it. Violence leaves marks even when you try to rinse it clean.

I raised my camera and took the shot, the click small and clinical in the damp.

“Who found him?” I asked, mostly to keep my mind in the present.

“Garbage pickup,” someone said. “Driver called it in.”

Of course. The alley was where the city threw away what it didn’t want to see.

I looked down once more. The victim’s open eye caught a sliver of light, glassy and unfocused, staring past the gate like it could still see a way out. A fly, confused by the cold, crawled along the edge of the eyelid and then stopped.

I didn’t close the eye. That wasn’t my job. My job was to read what was written here in rain and bruises and broken skin, and to keep my hands steady while I did it.

I capped my pen and slipped the notepad back into my coat.

“Let’s start the canvas,” I said, voice flat as the wet concrete. “And get me a list of anyone with access to that gate.”

The alley swallowed my words and gave nothing back. Only the drip, the distant traffic, and the thin, iron smell that clung to the back of my throat like a reminder: this was what people did to each other when they thought no one was looking, and it was my job to look anyway.

I leaned in, eyes doing the work my hands didn’t need to do yet. A fingernail. Not his. Too small, painted a chipped red. Someone had fought close enough to leave pieces behind. The alley kept souvenirs.

The smell of bleach drifted faintly under everything, thin and dishonest. Somebody had tried to clean, or at least to change the flavor of the air. It didn’t work. It never did. Blood doesn’t negotiate.

My gaze moved to the gate. The chain was new, bright steel against old rust. The padlock looked like it had been recently handled, fingerprints waiting in the moisture. On the ground beneath it, scuffed mud showed a hasty turn, heel marks overlapping, as if someone had hesitated and then decided not to go through.

I stood, slow. My joints complained in the cold, the kind of complaint that comes from too many nights like this. I didn’t let it reach my face.

There was a sound behind me—the faint, wet crunch of a boot on gravel. The medical examiner approached, hunched against the drizzle, kit in hand. Her eyes went straight to the body and didn’t flinch.

“Morning,” she said.

“It’s not,” I said, and flipped to a clean page.

She knelt beside the victim with the practiced care of someone working on a machine they’d repaired too often. She didn’t touch him yet, just looked. Her flashlight traced the bruising, the torn collar, the angle of the arm.

“Strangulation?” I asked.

“Likely,” she said. “And blunt force. See the swelling at the temple. He hit something hard. Wall, maybe. Ground. Could be both.”

The rain tapped the dumpster lid, a soft, impatient drumming. Somewhere a siren rose and faded, never coming closer. The city kept moving. It always kept moving.

I wrote: Ligature? No visible. Manual? Bruising suggests. Blunt trauma. The words sat in the notebook like they meant something solid. They were the closest thing to control.

My eyes went back to the victim’s hand. The fingers had dirt under the nails. Not alley dirt—lighter, sandy. Construction site, maybe. Or a park. It was a small detail, but small details were often the only honest ones.

“Any ID?” the uniform called from up the alley.

“Not yet,” I said.

I knew the routine. Bag the hands. Photograph every angle. Mark the evidence. Build a timeline from what water hadn’t washed away and what people would lie about later. There was a kind of comfort in procedure, if you could call it that—a rail to hold onto in a place where someone had died badly and the world expected you to make it make sense.

I stepped around the body, careful of the puddles that weren’t just puddles. Near the wall, under the smear, a faint print darkened the brick—a handprint, fingers spread, as if whoever did this had steadied themselves while they worked. The rain had softened it, but not erased it. Violence leaves marks even when you try to rinse it clean.

I raised my camera and took the shot, the click small and clinical in the damp.

“Who found him?” I asked, mostly to keep my mind in the present.

“Garbage pickup,” someone said. “Driver called it in.”

Of course. The alley was where the city threw away what it didn’t want to see.

I looked down once more. The victim’s open eye caught a sliver of light, glassy and unfocused, staring past the gate like it could still see a way out. A fly, confused by the cold, crawled along the edge of the eyelid and then stopped.

I didn’t close the eye. That wasn’t my job. My job was to read what was written here in rain and bruises and broken skin, and to keep my hands steady while I did it.

I capped my pen and slipped the notepad back into my coat.

“Let’s start the canvas,” I said, voice flat as the wet concrete. “And get me a list of anyone with access to that gate.”

The alley swallowed my words and gave nothing back. Only the drip, the distant traffic, and the thin, iron smell that clung to the back of my throat like a reminder: this was what people did to each other when they thought no one was looking, and it was my job to look anyway.

The courtyard had gone quiet in the way a room does when everyone is listening for something they don’t want to hear.

They’d marched him out with his hands bound and his shoulders already sagging, as if his body knew what was coming before his mind would admit it. The post stood at the center—old wood scarred by years of weather and use—its iron rings dull with age. The guard looped the rope through, cinched him forward, and stepped back without meeting his eyes.

Somewhere behind him leather slid through a palm: a slow, practiced sound, like a belt being drawn free. The whip made a faint, dry whisper as it uncoiled.

“Hold,” the officer said, not loudly. He didn’t need to raise his voice; the silence did the work for him.

The first strike didn’t sound like the crack people imagine from stories. It was heavier—more of a wet snap that seemed to punch the air out of the crowd. The prisoner jolted against the ropes, breath tearing out of him in a harsh, involuntary noise. For a heartbeat there was only the echo of impact and the creak of wood as he strained, then the guard let the whip fall slack again.

The second lash came faster, impatience in the motion. The leather sang on its way in—an ugly, thin hiss—then landed with a sharp report that made several heads flinch. He tried to swallow a cry and failed; it came out as a broken sound pressed into his teeth. His knees buckled and caught themselves, the rope holding him up when his legs wouldn’t.

“Count,” someone prompted.

He forced air into his lungs with a ragged gasp. “One,” he said, voice shaking, the word scraped out as if it cost him. “Two.”

The guard paced a half-circle behind him, measuring distance, resetting his stance. The whip’s handle thudded softly against the guard’s boot as he adjusted his grip, and that small, ordinary sound—wood on leather, leather on cloth—somehow made the next moment worse. It meant this was routine. It meant there was nothing personal in it to appeal to.

Another strike. Another. The rhythm established itself: hiss, snap, breath torn loose. Between blows, the prisoner’s shoulders trembled, and he fought to keep his head up, to keep counting, each number a small defiance dragged out of pain. The rope creaked as he shifted his weight, searching for any angle that hurt less and finding none.

The crowd stayed mostly silent, save for one muffled sob that was quickly swallowed. Even the birds had gone still. The only steady sounds were the guard’s measured steps and the whip’s hard punctuation, each crack followed by the prisoner’s strained breathing—fast and shallow now, as if his chest couldn’t decide whether to scream or pray.

By the time the officer lifted a hand to stop it, the prisoner’s voice had thinned to a rasp. He hung forward against the bindings, counting the last number more with stubbornness than strength, and the courtyard exhaled as one—no relief in it, only the instinctive release of people allowed to move again.

The guard coiled the whip with the same care he might have used for a length of rope. Leather slid over leather in a quiet, final rasp.

The prisoner sagged, eyes unfocused, listening to that sound as if it were the only proof the world hadn’t ended.

The cold had turned time into something thick and slow, like sap. Days blurred into a single long hour where hunger was the only clock that still worked.

He sat with his back against a piece of torn fuselage, knees drawn up, hands tucked into his armpits to keep the feeling in his fingers. The wind worried at the wreckage with a patient persistence, as if it could eventually pull the whole thing apart strand by strand. The others were quiet—not sleeping, not really talking—just saving what little warmth they had, saving words the way you saved calories.

The shape in the snow a few yards away had become, in his mind, two things at once: a person and an object. Both. Neither. He had watched his thoughts do it like a trick performed against his will. The mind, starving, began to categorize with brutal efficiency. *Food. Not food. Shelter. Danger.* It filed away names and memories because they were heavy, because reverence was heavy, because grief was heavy, and he could no longer afford weight that didn’t keep him alive.

Still, every time his eyes drifted that direction, something in his chest resisted, a small animal throwing itself against the bars. He tried to picture the person as they had been: laughter in the terminal, a complaint about the cramped seats, the easy assumption of tomorrow. The image came up weak, pale, like a photograph left out in the sun.

Someone had said it out loud earlier, the way you say something terrible when pretending it’s just practical information.

No one argued. They’d all passed beyond the stage where denial was noble. Denial had become a luxury.

But knowing and doing were different continents, separated by an ocean he did not know how to cross.

His stomach cramped hard enough to make him fold forward. It was not a polite emptiness. It was pain with a voice. It made everything else—shame, fear, the very idea of what kind of person he was—feel theoretical, like a lecture heard in another life. He pressed his forehead to his knees and breathed through his mouth, trying to outlast it. He thought: *I could die here.* And the thought was not dramatic. It was as plain as the sky.

The others watched him without looking like they were watching. That was part of the mercy: no one made it a ceremony. No one offered permission. No one said, “It’s okay.” Because it wasn’t, and they all knew it.

He stood up anyway.

His legs were unreliable, trembling with both weakness and the revolt of his own body against his decision. Each step felt like an argument. Snow squeaked under his boots in a sound that seemed too loud, too alive for what he was doing.

Up close, the boundary between person and object dissolved again and returned, dissolved and returned, like a blink. He found himself speaking in his head, not to the body in the snow, but to the memory of the person.

*I’m sorry. I’m sorry. I’m sorry.*

The words were useless. They did not build heat. They did not fill a stomach. They were only a rope thrown toward a cliff that had already crumbled.

His hands were clumsy with cold. He couldn’t bear to use his bare fingers. He used cloth, used the edge of something that had once been part of a seat, used anything that let him pretend there was distance between him and the act. He kept his eyes fixed on small, manageable details: the weave of fabric, the grain of metal, the way his breath formed a brief cloud and disappeared. If he looked up, if he allowed his mind to widen, he would fall into the full human shape of what he was doing and never move again.

When it was finally in his hands—a small portion, wrapped quickly, held like contraband—his brain seized on the final barrier: not the taking, but the eating. Until this point, it was still a plan, still logistics. The mouth made it real. The mouth made it him.

He returned to his spot and sat down, the others giving him space that was both kindness and self-preservation. He unwrapped what he’d brought with an unsteady care, like opening a letter he already knew would ruin him.

His mouth watered involuntarily, a betrayal so immediate it made his skin prickle with anger. His body did not care about the story he had been telling himself about decency. His body only recognized the possibility of continuing.

He held the piece near his lips and stopped.

There it was: the moment that demanded a new identity. He felt as if he were standing at a door with a sign he could read perfectly: *After this, you will remember yourself differently.* It wasn’t just the act that repulsed him—it was what it would mean. The collapse of the person he had believed he was. The knowledge that survival had a cost that could not be paid back.

His hands began to shake harder. Tears came, not with sobs, just with the silent leak of exhaustion and fear. He looked at the others. No one urged him. No one looked away. Their faces were gaunt masks of the same math he was doing: *One more day. One more hour. One more breath.*

He realized then that the breaking point wasn’t a sudden madness. It was a slow surrender of ideals to biology, inch by inch, until the remaining distance was so small you could mistake it for choice.

He thought of his mother—of the way she’d touch his cheek when he was sick, the way she’d say, *Eat something, you’ll feel better.* He thought of stupid, bright ordinary things: the smell of coffee, the bite of an apple, the way he’d once complained about being hungry as if hunger were an inconvenience rather than a threat. The memories were almost comical in their tenderness. They made his throat tighten.

Not heroically. Not purely. Not with an empty stomach and principles intact.

The first thing people noticed about Mercer’s house was how quiet it was.

Not the peaceful kind of quiet, the kind that makes you lower your voice because it feels like you’re interrupting something. The kind where even the air seems to be waiting for permission to move.

He’d bought the place because it was set back from the road and because the windows were tall enough to take in the light without letting the neighbors take him in. A collector needed privacy; a craftsman needed room.

Mercer liked that word—*craftsman*. It sanded down the uglier edges of the truth until he could hold it without cutting himself.

The downstairs was normal enough, if you didn’t look long: a sofa that had never been sat on like a person meant it, a kitchen with plates that matched because no one ever chipped them, a hallway whose family photos were all landscapes. No faces. No eyes following you. Just horizons and trees and blank, forgiving distance.

Upstairs was where the work lived.

He kept them there, in the long room under the peaked roof, where the ceiling beams made an insect-like ribcage above his head. He called it his gallery, though no one was ever invited. Against the far wall, beneath the skylight, his collection stood in permanent poses that suggested life had paused, not ended.

A woman in a lavender dress held one palm out as if to test rain.

A man in a suit leaned with patient familiarity against a mantel that had never hosted a fire.

A teenager sat cross-legged on a low stool, chin lifted, a look on his face that could almost be called amused if you didn’t stare at the fixedness of it.

Mercer had dressed them carefully. He had brushed their hair and chosen fabrics that would not fade too fast in the sun, that would age with dignity. He had arranged hands and fingers as if the smallest gesture could pass for personality. Sometimes he would stand in the doorway and wait for his mind to supply the missing warmth, the missing breath. Sometimes, when the house settled, he could almost pretend it had.

It wasn’t the killing that held him, not really. Killing was a doorway, and doorways were ugly. It was what came after that he understood: the stillness you could shape. The silence you could preserve. The way a person’s chaos—anger, joy, cruelty, laughter—could be made neat if you were meticulous enough.

On the night he brought the newest one home, the rain came down in straight, unwavering lines, as if the sky were stitching the world shut.

He carried the body like something valuable, wrapped against the weather. His hands were steady, practiced. He had long ago learned what shaking meant: not guilt, but impatience.

In his studio—the small room off the gallery that smelled faintly of varnish and antiseptic—he laid the bundle on the central table. Everything in that room had its place. Nothing there was sentimental. It was the opposite of a shrine; it was a workshop.

He didn’t turn on the overhead light right away. He preferred the lamp that cast a warmer circle, the kind of glow that made harsh things seem domestic. For a moment he stood and listened, letting his breathing match the slow tick of the clock. He told himself the same thing he always told himself at the beginning: *Take your time. Do it properly. Make it last.*

When he finally peeled back the covering, the victim’s face appeared in the lamplight—slack, emptied of intention. The features were ordinary enough, which was usually what drew Mercer in. Ordinary people were more convincing as art; there was less to compete with. No one expected brilliance from a stranger.

He studied the face as if it might argue with him. “You’ll be better this way,” he said softly, and the quiet of the room accepted the lie without comment.

He worked with ritualistic care, not in the lurid hurry of violence but in the deliberate cadence of someone performing a task he had rehearsed a thousand times in his head. There were steps he would not name out loud, even to himself, because naming them made them too real, too physical. Better to think in abstractions: *preparation*, *preservation*, *finishing*. Better to reduce the human to stages.

The first stage was always about erasing what time would do. He had learned early that death was not a still frame; it was a process, and it fought him. His whole craft was a war against decay: against sagging, slackening, darkening. Against the way the body insists on becoming evidence rather than object.

He cleaned, adjusted, tended—less like a butcher than a fastidious tailor trying to make a suit sit right on a mannequin. There was an intimacy to it that he refused to recognize as intimacy. He never kissed his work; he never wept over it. He only corrected.

As he progressed, he began to make choices. That, to Mercer, was the true art: deciding what a person would be when they could no longer decide for themselves.

He tested the angle of the head, lifted the chin, lowered it again. The face, left alone, wanted to be simply dead; Mercer wanted it to be *suggestive*. A hint of thought. A whisper of emotion.

He settled on something close to curiosity—an expression that would make a visitor, if there ever were one, lean in and wonder what the figure was looking at.

He changed the clothes, too. The victim had arrived in something unremarkable, something that belonged to a life Mercer had not cared about. He chose instead a cream-colored sweater from his storage trunk, the kind that looked soft and clean even in dim light. He liked the contrast: warmth implied by fabric, cold guaranteed by truth.

When the body was ready to be moved—ready to join the others—Mercer paused to wipe his hands and check his reflection in the darkened window. His hair was neat, his face unremarkable. That was one of the small mercies of the world: it offered anonymity to anyone who wanted it enough.

He carried the finished figure into the gallery with the same reverence a museum worker might give a sculpture. He positioned it near the skylight where the daylight could do half the work of convincing: soft shadows, gentle highlights, the illusion of breath in the rise of a chest that would never rise again.

Then he stepped back.

In the row of preserved lives, the new addition looked almost plausible—almost like a person caught mid-thought, interrupted by the sudden call of a name from another room.

Mercer folded his arms and allowed himself a thin satisfaction. He imagined, as he always did, what it would be like for someone to stumble into this place unprepared. To see the collection and feel, for a few heartbeats, that dizzy confusion: *Are they real?*

He loved that moment. Not because it frightened people—though it would—but because it proved his point. That he could take what was messy and fleeting and make it *stay*.

Downstairs, the house creaked as the temperature shifted. The rain on the roof softened to a whisper.

Mercer went from one figure to the next, making small adjustments: a wrist turned a fraction, a collar smoothed, a strand of hair tucked back into place. He spoke to them sometimes, not because he believed they could hear, but because the sound of his own voice made the room feel occupied.

“You’re safe now,” he murmured, moving to the new one. “No more choices. No more mistakes.”

In the quiet, the gallery seemed to watch him watch them, a hall of borrowed faces and stolen stillness. For a moment, Mercer felt something he almost recognized as peace.

Then, faintly, from somewhere he couldn’t place—maybe the vents, maybe the bones of the house itself—came a sound like a soft, wet inhale.

He froze.

The figures did not move. Their eyes did not shift. Their hands remained where he had arranged them. Yet the feeling in the room changed, as if the air had thickened with a presence that wasn’t his.

Mercer swallowed, suddenly aware of his own heartbeat, loud and rude in the stillness.

He had built this place to be a sanctuary from time, from consequence, from the unbearable fact that everything living insists on changing. He had filled it with his proof that permanence could be made.

But standing among his collection, he felt—just for an instant—that permanence wasn’t the same as control.

And that the quiet he loved so much wasn’t empty.

It was listening.

The room smelled like wet pennies and old bleach.

Jalen’s wrists burned where the cuffs bit into him, the metal cold enough to feel *alive* against his skin. Every time he flexed, the chain answered with a tight, impatient rattle, like the machine was clearing its throat.

In front of him, a stainless-steel bowl sat on a pedestal under a cone of light. The rest of the room was swallowed by shadow, but the bowl shone—too clean, too deliberate—except for what moved inside it.

A thin skittering sound rose and fell in waves.

Jalen leaned forward despite himself, throat tightening before he was even close. In the bowl were dark, glossy shapes, packed together in a writhing mound. Some clung to the sides. Others crawled over each other in a frantic, soundless panic. The smell wasn’t quite rot, not quite earth—more like damp leaves left in a sealed bag too long, sour and sharp at the back of his nose.

A speaker crackled overhead.

“Hello, Jalen.”

The voice was calm, conversational, the kind of tone you might use to explain a parking ticket. That made it worse.

“You’ve spent years taking what you wanted and letting others choke on the consequences. Today, you will learn what it means to swallow your choices.”

The chain on his right wrist suddenly jerked. A mechanical arm at the edge of his vision rotated into place, ending in a broad, rubber-lined clamp—positioned perfectly to force his jaw open if it engaged.

Jalen’s mouth went dry so fast his tongue felt like cloth.

On the pedestal, a digital timer blinked to life: **02:00**.

Beside the bowl, a clear tube ran from the pedestal down into the floor, like a drain. A small placard was bolted to the metal: **EMPTY THE BOWL TO STOP THE TIMER.**

His stomach turned hard, an instinctive, full-body recoil as if gravity had shifted inside him.

“No,” he breathed, and the word came out thin.

The speaker hissed again. “You have two minutes. If the bowl is not empty, the clamp will engage. After that, the device will do the eating for you.”

Jalen swallowed and regretted it immediately—his throat tried to reject the motion, like even the idea of swallowing had become hostile. Saliva flooded in late, bitter with adrenaline.

He pulled against the cuffs once, twice, the metal cutting into skin. The bowl didn’t move. The timer didn’t care.

**01:43.**

He stared at the mass in the bowl, willing it to stop moving, to become *food* in some comprehensible way. His brain kept throwing up images that made his stomach lurch: texture, legs, the way they’d feel against his tongue.

His gag reflex fired early, a dry heave that punched up from his diaphragm and left him blinking with tears. He tried to breathe through his nose, but the smell filled his skull, thick and unavoidable.

**01:29.**

“Think,” he told himself, voice shaking. “Just—don’t think.”

He reached his face toward the bowl as if he were approaching a wound. The light made the shapes shine. A few crawled onto the rim, searching for escape.

His tongue curled back against his teeth, refusing. His jaw clenched so hard it ached. Another involuntary retch climbed up and he swallowed it down with a whimper.

He pinched his eyes shut, grabbed a fistful with trembling fingers—warm, living, wrong—and brought it to his lips.

The first touch was enough.

His mouth tried to recoil on its own, lips pulling back, jaw locking. He forced it open with a sound that was half sob, half snarl. The shapes pressed against his tongue and his entire body surged in revolt.

He gagged hard, shoulders jerking against the restraints. The world narrowed to the brutal rhythm of **don’t throw up, don’t throw up** and the timer’s relentless blinking behind his eyelids.

He tried to chew because he didn’t know what else to do, and the sensation—soft in some places, sharp in others—sent nausea skyrocketing. He swallowed with a violent spasm, throat working like it was pushing down something that had hooks.

Instantly, his stomach cramped in protest.

“Again,” he gasped, not to the voice, but to himself. “Again.”

The temple breathed cold stone and old incense. Columns rose like petrified trees, their carvings worn smooth by centuries of hands that had come here to plead, to bargain, to disappear. Somewhere in the dark above, a slow drip counted time with indifferent patience.

At the center lay the altar—black, polished, and faintly reflective, as if it refused to hold light for long. A ring of candles surrounded it, their flames steady despite the drafts that prowled the corridors. The air tasted of metal and ash.

The priest entered without ceremony. No grand gesture, no chant to announce his importance. He moved with the economy of someone performing a task he had repeated so often it no longer required thought. His robe was immaculate, its hem never touching the floor; his hands were clean, nails trimmed, skin pale as if daylight had never claimed him.

The victim was brought forward—bound, unsteady, eyes wide and searching for mercy in faces that did not offer it. The acolytes kept their gaze lowered, not from reverence but from habit. Chains shifted softly. A muffled whimper broke and was swallowed by the temple’s vast, listening dark.

The priest did not look at the victim as a person. His eyes passed over the trembling body the way a mason examines stone—measuring, judging, preparing. He checked the bindings with a brief tug, as if testing a knot before a journey. When the victim’s breath hitched into something like a sob, the priest’s expression remained unchanged: neither cruel nor kind, simply absent.

He took up the ritual blade from its resting place. It was not ornate. It did not need to be. The metal caught candlelight and gave it back in a thin, cold line. The priest held it with a practiced grip, adjusting his fingers once, precisely, the way a scribe settles a pen.

Words began—ancient syllables that scraped against the air like stone against stone. The priest spoke them evenly, without emphasis, without fervor. There was no anger to give them heat, no joy to lend them music. His voice was a tool: steady, reliable, unfeeling. Each phrase landed in the chamber and seemed to sink into the floor, as if the temple itself were drinking.

The victim struggled; the altar answered with a dull thud of restraints. Another sound followed—raw, involuntary—cut short as the acolytes tightened their hold. The priest did not pause. He did not flinch. He did not hurry, either. He waited for the body to still into exhaustion, not out of compassion but because the ritual required order.

When the blade moved, it did so with clinical certainty. The motion was quick and controlled, performed at a practiced angle, with the detached precision of a butcher who refuses to waste effort. The victim’s cry rose—high, broken, then dissolving into ragged breaths.

The candles shivered as if something unseen had exhaled across them.

The priest watched with the same expression he might wear while observing water pour into a cup. No triumph. No disgust. Not even curiosity. His eyes remained flat, and his mouth held a neutral line, as though emotion were an unnecessary ornament in a place that demanded only function.

The air thickened. The shadows seemed to deepen, gathering in the corners like an audience leaning closer. The priest continued the chant at the same measured pace, never raising his voice, never letting the tremor in someone else’s suffering disturb the cadence. Whatever was being offered here—life, breath, fear—it was offered with the calm of a transaction.

When it was over, the priest cleaned the blade with a cloth folded neatly in his palm. He did it carefully, methodically, removing every trace with the mild impatience of someone wiping dust from glass. He set the knife back in its place and adjusted the candles so their ring was unbroken.

Only then did he look upward, not to heaven, but to the darkness above the altar.

His face remained empty.

The alley has its own kind of dusk, even at midday—light trapped between brick walls, strained through a grate of fire escapes and laundry lines. It’s thinner now, that light. It used to have edges. It used to cut the world into shapes I could name.

I’m on my side, cheek against wet concrete, and the light above me is paling like a television losing signal. The sky is a narrow strip, a blade of gray. It sways when I blink, or maybe I’m the one swaying. My eyelids feel heavy in the way a door does when it’s been warped by rain.

Somewhere behind my ribs, there’s a sound that is only mine.

Thump.

It’s not loud, not the way I always imagined your heart would be when you’re afraid. It’s a private noise, the kind you feel in your throat when you swallow, in your wrists when you’re feverish. It thuds up through my chest and into my ears, and for a second the whole alley seems to pulse with it. Like the world is keeping time for me.

Thump.

I try to breathe deep and my body refuses, like it’s offended by the suggestion. The air comes in shallow, quick sips. It tastes like metal and old rainwater and whatever the city sweats out when nobody’s looking.

My hand is pressed hard against my side. It’s a habit more than a choice, the way you press on a door that’s trying to swing open. The warmth under my palm is wrong—too slick, too eager to leave. When I shift my fingers, the skin of my glove drags and sticks. I stop moving them.

The fight is already fading, not as a memory but as a sensation. My arms don’t remember the weight of the knife. My knuckles don’t remember hitting teeth. The adrenaline has peeled away, leaving everything exposed and quiet. The sounds that are left are small ones: water dripping from a pipe. A distant car door. Someone’s laughter far enough away that it might as well be another city.

And my heartbeat.

Thump.

Thump.

It’s slower now, or maybe it’s just that everything else has stopped rushing. Each beat feels like a question my body keeps asking: Are we still here? Are we still here? And each answer is less sure.

Cold is the next thing to arrive.

It begins where the concrete touches me, seeping through my coat, finding the points of bone—hip, shoulder, the side of my face. It spreads upward in thin, patient fingers. My legs are still warm, I think. Or they were. It’s hard to tell where I end and the alley begins. The air is colder than it should be. Or my blood is warmer than it should be leaving me.

I blink again and the strip of sky narrows. The light is still there, but it looks farther away, as if someone is drawing a curtain and I’m watching from the wrong side of the glass. The bricks opposite me have lost their color. Everything is the same shade of tired.

Thump.

There’s a moment—small, almost polite—where my body tries to do something sensible. A shiver crawls through me, starting in my spine and breaking apart in my shoulders. It’s like a signal flare, the last of the automatic responses. After it passes, I feel… less. Not less pain. Less weight. Less urgency. Like the cords holding me to my muscles are loosening one by one.

Pain is a bright thing at first, a hot knot that sits in my side and insists on being noticed. But it’s fading too, not vanishing so much as drifting away from me, floating a few inches out of reach. I can still sense it, like a light behind a wall. I could reach for it if I wanted. I don’t.

My breath fogs faintly when it leaves me. I watch it go, a small ghost. It dissolves into the alley air without argument.

Thump.

Thump.

The rhythm is wrong now. There’s a drag between beats, an empty space that feels larger than it should. My ears fill with the sound, then the hush. Sound, hush. Like waves pulling back from shore.

I try to lift my head. My neck trembles and gives up. The motion makes the world smear; the sky becomes a streak, the fire escape a ladder of black lines. When the image settles, the light seems dimmer, though I’m not sure if the sun has moved or my eyes are simply tired of seeing.

There’s something wet under my shoulder blade. It’s growing colder by the second, cooling like spilled tea. It should alarm me. It does, a little, in a distant way. The part of me that knows numbers and consequences looks at the situation and begins to tally. The rest of me just listens.

Thump.

I think of the other person’s face—how close it was, how anonymous. Teeth bared, eyes wide, the flash of steel. It’s already turning into a story someone else could tell. I can’t hold onto the details. I don’t have the strength to keep them sharp. Memory is a fist that’s opening.

The alley smells like damp stone and trash, and underneath that, my own iron smell, thick and intimate. I inhale and it fills me with something like nausea, something like peace. My body is making a quiet decision.

The cold has reached my hands. My fingers are stiff, curled around nothing. I try to make them move and they answer slowly, as if they have to travel a great distance to obey.

Thump.

There’s a flicker at the edge of my vision, a bright shimmer like sunlight on water. For a heartbeat I think it’s someone coming—footsteps, a shadow at the mouth of the alley. But it’s only my eyes, or my brain, or whatever part of me is beginning to disconnect. The world is fraying at its borders.

The light above is thinner still. The strip of sky is no longer a blade but a thread. It trembles.

My breath slows. The inhale feels optional. The exhale feels like letting go of something I didn’t realize I was holding.

Thump.

The sound of my heart is no longer inside my chest; it’s everywhere, filling the alley like a drum heard through a wall. Each beat arrives with effort, and then the silence that follows it is deeper than the one before. The gaps between beats are growing longer, stretching, yawning open.

Thump.

I wait for the next one, the way you wait for a friend who is late. The way you stare at a door and listen for the hinge.

The light dims again. Or my eyes close. It’s hard to tell when the world is fading in such small increments, when the end arrives not as a slam but as a slow, careful lowering.

My cheek is cold against the concrete. My mouth is slack. The taste of metal is gone, replaced by nothing at all.

Somewhere inside me, a final beat gathers itself.

Thump.

And then there is a hush so complete it feels like stepping into snow.

The cold has reached my hands. My fingers are stiff, curled around nothing. I try to make them move and they answer slowly, as if they have to travel a great distance to obey.

Thump.

There’s a flicker at the edge of my vision, a bright shimmer like sunlight on water. For a heartbeat I think it’s someone coming—footsteps, a shadow at the mouth of the alley. But it’s only my eyes, or my brain, or whatever part of me is beginning to disconnect. The world is fraying at its borders.

The light above is thinner still. The strip of sky is no longer a blade but a thread. It trembles.

My breath slows. The inhale feels optional. The exhale feels like letting go of something I didn’t realize I was holding.

Thump.

The sound of my heart is no longer inside my chest; it’s everywhere, filling the alley like a drum heard through a wall. Each beat arrives with effort, and then the silence that follows it is deeper than the one before. The gaps between beats are growing longer, stretching, yawning open.

Thump.

I wait for the next one, the way you wait for a friend who is late. The way you stare at a door and listen for the hinge.

The light dims again. Or my eyes close. It’s hard to tell when the world is fading in such small increments, when the end arrives not as a slam but as a slow, careful lowering.

My cheek is cold against the concrete. My mouth is slack. The taste of metal is gone, replaced by nothing at all.

Somewhere inside me, a final beat gathers itself.

Thump.

And then there is a hush so complete it feels like stepping into snow.

The house smelled like wet carpet and old heat, the kind of stale warmth that clung to everything after the power had been shut off. Detective Mara Ellery paused in the entryway, letting her eyes adjust, letting the silence settle on her shoulders like a hand.

Behind her, an officer murmured into a radio. Somewhere down the hall, a floorboard gave a tired creak as if the building itself wanted to confess.

Mara followed the thin trail of disturbance through the living room: a toppled lamp, a picture frame facedown, a scatter of stuffing like spilled snow along the baseboard. The dog toys—bright, chewed rubber—looked obscene against the gray carpet.

In the kitchen doorway she stopped. The light from her flashlight cut across the table and landed on a small, careful arrangement: a cereal bowl rinsed clean and set upside down on a towel, a child’s plastic cup aligned beside it, and a folded piece of notebook paper placed dead center as if it had been measured.

Not tossed. Not hidden. Presented.

Mara’s gloved fingers lifted the note by its corner. The paper was ruled wide, the kind used in elementary classrooms, and it smelled faintly of crayons and dish soap. The handwriting was neat and rounded, practiced, with a few letters traced over as if the writer needed them to be perfect.

She read.

---

**DEAR WHOEVER FINDS THIS,**

**I’M NOT SORRY LIKE YOU WANT ME TO BE. I TRIED TO BE BUT IT DIDN’T FIT.**

**YOU WILL THINK I’M MEAN. YOU WILL SAY “POOR BABY” ABOUT HIM. YOU WILL SAY “WHAT KIND OF CHILD DOES THAT.”**

**A CHILD WHO LISTENS.**

**HE WAS GOOD. HE LICKED MY HANDS EVEN WHEN THEY SMELLED LIKE PENNIES. HE FOLLOWED ME LIKE I WAS THE SUN AND HE WAS A PLANET. I LOVED HIM THE WAY YOU LOVE A SONG YOU PUT ON REPEAT UNTIL IT STARTS TO HURT.**

**BUT HE STARTED TO KNOW.**

**IT WAS IN HIS EYES FIRST. HE WOULD LOOK PAST ME, NOT AT ME, LIKE SOMETHING WAS STANDING BEHIND MY HEAD AND HE WAS TRYING NOT TO MAKE IT MAD. WHEN THE HOUSE GOT QUIET HE WOULD PUT HIS EARS UP AND STARE AT THE HALLWAY AND HIS WHOLE BODY WOULD GO TIGHT LIKE A STRING.**

**HE GROWLED AT THE AIR.**

**THE AIR DOESN’T DO THINGS FOR NO REASON.**

**MOM SAID HE WAS “JUST A DOG.” DAD SAID I “WATCH TOO MANY MOVIES.” TEACHER SAID I HAVE “BIG FEELINGS.”**

**THEY DON’T HEAR IT.**

**AT NIGHT, WHEN I’M IN BED AND THE DOOR IS CLOSED, I CAN HEAR THE HOUSE BREATHING. IT BREATHES AROUND THE WINDOWS AND UNDER THE FLOOR. SOMETIMES IT SAYS MY NAME IN THE VOICE I’M GOING TO HAVE WHEN I’M GROWN UP. SOMETIMES IT DOESN’T USE A VOICE. IT JUST PUSHES THOUGHTS INTO MY HEAD LIKE THUMBS.**

**IT SAID HE WOULD TELL.**

**NOT WITH WORDS. WITH HIS BODY. WITH HIS BARKING. WITH HIS FEAR. HE WOULD MAKE THEM LOOK. HE WOULD MAKE THEM ASK QUESTIONS. AND THEN THEY WOULD FIND OUT I’M NOT EMPTY INSIDE LIKE I’M SUPPOSED TO BE.**

**I TRIED TO MAKE HIM STOP WATCHING THE HALL. I TRIED TO COVER HIS EYES WITH MY HANDS AND SAY IT WAS OKAY. I TRIED TO BE SO SOFT THAT NOTHING BAD COULD GET THROUGH ME.**

**BUT HE KEPT LISTENING.**

**AND THEN IT SAID IF I DIDN’T, IT WOULD DO IT ANYWAY AND IT WOULD USE ME LIKE A HAND.**

**SO I DID IT MYSELF. THAT’S DIFFERENT. WHEN YOU DO IT YOURSELF YOU GET TO CHOOSE WHERE THE END IS.**

**I WAS QUIET. I WAS GENTLE. I TALKED TO HIM THE WHOLE TIME SO HE WOULDN’T BE ALONE IN HIS LAST MINUTE. I TOLD HIM HE WAS THE BEST BOY AND THAT I’M SORRY HE HAD TO BE BRAVE. I TOLD HIM THANK YOU FOR LOVING ME EVEN WHEN YOU COULD SEE THE THING THAT LOVES ME BACK.**

**YOU WILL LOOK FOR MONSTERS. YOU WILL LOOK FOR ME TOO.**

**YOU WON’T HAVE TO LOOK HARD.**

**I’M LEARNING HOW TO BE VERY GOOD AT WHAT I HAVE TO DO.**

**PLEASE FEED THE FISH. THEY DIDN’T DO ANYTHING YET.**

**— E.**

---

Mara lowered the paper slowly, as if moving too fast might startle the room into sound.

Behind her, the radio crackled again, too loud in the tight house. She didn’t answer it. Her eyes stayed on the last line, the one that seemed almost polite, almost normal, and therefore worse than the rest.

A child who underlined their own name. A child who arranged a bowl and cup like place settings, like they were expecting company. A child who wrote *yet* as if it was part of a schedule.

Mara set the note back down exactly where she’d found it.

Her flashlight beam drifted to the corner of the kitchen where a small aquarium sat dark and still, the water line low. A faint tapping came from inside the glass—slow, patient, like someone knocking from the other side.

Mara swallowed, lifted her radio, and finally spoke.

“Dispatch,” she said, keeping her voice steady because the house felt like it was listening. “Tell Animal Control to check for live pets. And get me every school record you can on a child with the initial E. Start with the nearest elementary.”

Her eyes moved to the hallway the note had mentioned, a strip of deeper shadow beyond the kitchen light.

She couldn’t shake the feeling that the note wasn’t a confession.

It was an invitation.

---

The mercenary paused at the threshold, letting the door hang half-open on its hinges. Beyond it, the room was a low-ceilinged storage bay turned killbox—stacked crates, dangling conduit, a single strip light flickering like a failing pulse.

He raised the flamethrower and felt the weight of it settle into his shoulders. The hose tugged at the tank on his back with every breath. Even before he fired, the air tasted wrong—stale, oily, thick with dust and old chemicals.

A voice barked inside. Boots scuffed. A weapon clattered against metal.

He squeezed the trigger.

The ignition coughed, then the nozzle spat a roaring tongue of fire that filled the doorway with a sudden, living brightness. Heat slammed into him like a physical force, pushing against his face shield and seeping through the seams of his gear. The room’s shadows vanished in an instant, replaced by wild, writhing light that bounced off the walls and made everything look too close.

The flame rolled outward and upward, licking across stacked pallets and crawling along the ceiling. The air itself seemed to curl and shrink away, oxygen snatched and consumed. Plastic shrieked as it warped. Paint blistered. A crackle rose into a relentless, hungry roar.

Then came the screaming—sharp and immediate, the kind that didn’t come from a plan or a fight, only from panic. It echoed off metal shelving and concrete, multiplying, turning the small space into a chamber of sound.

He stepped in, sweeping the nozzle in short arcs. Not a spray—an erase. Fire moved where he guided it, bright and indiscriminate. Smoke ballooned fast, rolling in thick, greasy layers that stung his eyes even through the mask. The smell turned bitter and choking—burned fuel, scorched fabric, chemicals cooking off—an acrid, sickening mix that clung to the back of his throat.

Someone fired blindly. Muzzle flashes winked through the smoke like fireflies, brief and useless. Rounds snapped into the doorframe, pinged off a steel cabinet, vanished into the haze.

He kept moving, methodical, using the wall as a reference point. The heat kept building, trapped by the low ceiling. Sweat ran down his spine. The flamethrower’s roar vibrated through his arms, and the tank on his back felt hotter with each passing second, like it was remembering what it carried.

A figure burst from behind a shelf, half-seen in the orange wash, hands up, mouth open—another scream swallowed by the roaring flame and the crackling room. The mercenary didn’t slow. He angled the stream to cut off the escape path instead of chasing it, herding the panic back into the smoke.

The strip light above flickered once, twice, then died. Firelight took over completely—unstable and feral. The room shrank into a tunnel of heat and noise.

When he released the trigger, the sudden absence of sound was almost worse. The roar dropped away, leaving only the snap of small fires and the hiss of something leaking. The smoke continued to roll, thick as fog, carrying that scorched, chemical stink that made his stomach tighten.

In the dim, the remaining movement was frantic and blind—coughing, stumbling, scraping against concrete. The mercenary adjusted his stance, thumbed the trigger again, and the flame answered with another burst of daylight.

The screams rose once more, then were swallowed by the crackle and the consuming heat as he cleared the last corners, one sweep at a time.

results.model_response:
At first, it’s easy for them to pretend it’s stress.

They wake with crescent-shaped flakes on the sheets, like dandruff scaled up to something obscene. Their skin has always been a little dry in winter; that’s what they tell themselves as they rub lotion into their forearms until it pills and smears. But the dryness isn’t dryness. It’s separation. The surface of them is loosening from the person underneath, lifting at the edges in thin, translucent petals that catch on clothing and peel back when they move.

In the bathroom mirror, they watch their own body betray the rules it used to follow. Their knuckles look too big, the skin around them stretched and glossy, as if the bones beneath are trying to press through. The lines on their palms have gone pale, as though the hands are preparing to belong to something that doesn’t need fingerprints.

The shedding comes in phases. First the soft places—inside the elbows, behind the knees, where sweat gathers. Then the torso, sheets of skin loosening in wide, wet panels that make their stomach lurch when they tug and feel it give with the resistance of tape. Underneath is newer skin: slick, faintly iridescent, not raw exactly, but wrong. It doesn’t quite match their blood, doesn’t blush or freckle, doesn’t respond to heat. It looks manufactured, as if their body is rebuilding itself out of unfamiliar materials.

They learn to fear showers. Water helps it come away faster.

Sometimes, after, they find scraps caught in the drain like pale seaweed, and they stand there, trembling, with a hand over their mouth, trying not to gag—not from the sight, but from the relief. Relief that it’s off. Relief that it’s happening. Relief that the old layer is gone.

The bones start later, but they are less forgiving.

It begins as an ache deep in the jaw, like a molar infection. Then a pressure in the cheekbones, a tightness behind the eyes. They hold their face between both hands and feel it subtly misalign, the way wood swells and twists with moisture. Their bite changes. Teeth click differently. The shape of their tongue feels wrong inside their mouth, too large, too crowded.

The first real break happens in the night.

They’re half-asleep when their arm spasms, and the sound is not the clean crack of a snapped branch but a wet, intimate pop—cartilage and ligament protesting, then surrendering. Pain bursts bright enough to bleach their thoughts, and they sit upright, panting, clutching their forearm, expecting to find it bent at a sick angle.

It isn’t.

The skin bulges. Something shifts under it, sliding as if the bone has decided it wants a different route through the body. The pain comes in waves as the internal structure rearranges: old joints dissolving, new ones knitting. They can feel the grit of it—the sensation of something grinding down to make room, then the slow, nauseating pressure of rebuilding.

Over the next days, their posture changes. Their shoulders sit slightly farther back, as though a new hinge has been installed. Their spine aches in a precise line, each vertebra throbbing like it’s being turned by an unseen hand. When they bend, they hear faint clicks that weren’t there before, like a lock being tested.

They become cautious about movement, then reckless. One afternoon, frustrated and sweating, they brace both hands against a doorframe and pull, trying to stretch out the ache in their ribs.

A rib snaps.

They gasp, stumble, and laugh—an ugly, involuntary bark that surprises them more than the pain. Because the pain is real, sharp, and intense… but it doesn’t carry warning anymore. It doesn’t persuade. It doesn’t teach.

Within hours the broken place feels… better. Not healed—revised. The rib sits differently, higher, as if their body has been sketching a new blueprint and finally got permission to erase the old lines.

Their reflection becomes an argument they keep losing. The face is still theirs in the way a childhood photograph is still yours—recognizable, but belonging to a time that cannot be recovered. The eyes sit a fraction wider apart. The nose bridge seems flatter. The lips pull back from the teeth when they’re not paying attention, an unconscious tension that bares more enamel than a smile should.

People ask if they’ve lost weight.

They say yes, because it’s the closest lie they have. They’re not losing weight; they’re losing proportions, losing the math of a human body. Their clothes hang wrong, sleeves riding up as forearms lengthen by millimeters that add up, collars tugging uncomfortably at a throat that seems thicker, more corded. Their nails harden into something more like horn, and when one breaks it doesn’t bleed—it splinters.

The worst part isn’t the pain. It’s how quickly they adapt to it.

At the start, every change is a horror, an emergency. They take pictures, they make notes, they search for answers at three in the morning with shaking hands. They draft messages to doctors and delete them because how do you explain your bones are rebuilding like they’ve remembered a different species?

Then the body starts winning small negotiations with the mind.

They stop taking pictures because the images make them nauseous, not from fear but from impatience. The camera never catches the important part—the way their muscles flex a second too long, the way tendons seem to tighten on their own, testing strength. The way their skin, new and sleek, doesn’t goosebump.

They stop making notes because writing feels slow. Their thoughts are beginning to align into simpler categories: warm/cold, safe/not safe, mine/not mine. Words become decorative.

The moral compass goes the same way—quietly, at first.

They don’t wake up and decide to be cruel. Cruelty is still, in theory, a thing they dislike. It’s just that the mechanisms that used to enforce kindness begin to loosen, like their skin. Guilt doesn’t cling the way it once did. It slides off.

The first time they do something wrong, it’s small: they see a neighbor’s cat perched on a fence, watching them with bright, indifferent eyes. They raise a hand to shoo it away, and the cat flinches—too slow. Their fingers close around its scruff with an ease that shocks them, a grip stronger than it should be. The cat yowls, claws scrabbling, and their heartbeat slows.

Not with calm.

With focus.

They let it go, eventually, because the sound of its distress draws a curtain twitching across the street. They set it down gently, even. They watch it sprint away.

And they realize, with a cold clarity, that what stopped them wasn’t compassion.

It was inconvenience.

After that, the world rearranges itself around new priorities. When someone bumps into them on the train and mutters an apology, they don’t automatically forgive; they assess. When a coworker cries in the break room, they don’t feel the old reflex to comfort; they feel irritation at the noise, at the wetness, at the time being wasted. The sound of sobbing registers like a high-pitched mechanical failure.

They begin to notice things they used to ignore: the pulsing in throats, the soft give of bellies under fabric, the delicate architecture of joints. Their eyes track movement with predatory patience.
